metadata.name: Tend verified rules
metadata.description: The verified rules in Tend's law library, for the crime victim compensation programs of the 50 states and DC. Each rule has a plain-language summary and a verbatim quote from a saved source, with its pinpoint citation, address, and sha256.
metadata.not_legal_advice: Tend is not legal advice. It shows what each program's own rules say, with the quote. The program decides.

jurisdictions.name: Alaska

program.agency: Alaska Department of Public Safety, Violent Crimes Compensation Board

coverage.notes: exam_payment: AS 18.68.040 bars charging survivors 16 and older (including through their insurance) but does not name who pays, and no official source I saved names the payer. minimum_loss: no minimum loss found in AS 18.67 or on the VCCB site. Reporting: AS 18.67.130(a)(2) requires a police report within five days (or five days after a report could reasonably be made); no anonymous-report, forensic-exam, or advocate alternative for compensation was found, even though AS 18.68.020 lets adults choose an anonymous report for the exam itself. No VCCB administrative regulations were found; the program's Statutes and Policies page cites only AS 18.67 and federal VOCA. Expense caps come from the VCCB Benefits at a Glance PDF (July 2026), which says it does not supplement or contradict the statutes. Transportation: Benefits at a Glance caps transportation at $5,000 per major event (funeral, trial, etc.); that cap is not stored as a rule because per-event is not one of the schema's per values. processing_time: no VCCB page, the application, or AS 18.67 states a time for a decision or payment; AS 18.67.040 only gives the applicant 30 days to request a hearing after an unfavorable decision.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Deadline disagreement: AS 18.67.130(a)(1) says two years after the injury; the application PDF says within 2 years of the crime or discovery of the crime, and the home page asks applicants past two years to explain the delay. The statute wins, so the rule uses two years from the crime. AS 18.68.040 covers survivors of sexual assault under AS 11.41.410 to 11.41.425 who are 16 or older; younger survivors are not addressed by that section. Benefits at a Glance caps were checked against the PDF's column layout (pdftotext -layout) so each amount is tied to the right expense row. The Benefits at a Glance funeral row mentions up to $10,000 in emergency consideration across two applications; the statute caps one emergency award at $5,000, which is what the rule uses. The OVC directory lists the program under the Alaska Department of Public Safety, phone 800-764-3040; the VCCB home page lists the same toll-free number. Lost wages: up to two weeks without a provider note, longer with medical justification (Benefits at a Glance). Reviewer: chiropractic's $3,500 limit is stored under expense 'other' so it is not read as the medical cap; Benefits at a Glance lists general medical expenses at up to $40,000, the same as the total cap. The application's eligibility list says reasonable exceptions may apply to its requirements (police report within 5 days, 2-year filing), but no source says what those exceptions are. How to file: the application page lists online, mail, and fax; the application's instructions say it can be submitted by mail, email, or fax and give VCCB@alaska.gov; the home page calls it secure email. The online rule's target is vccb.alaska.gov because that is what the instructions print; the portal itself is https://application.vccb.alaska.gov/ (program.apply_url, linked from the application page). Documents: police report, bills, receipts, and insurance information are asked for if available, and the instructions say not to wait for them before applying; only the signed Release of Information is required with every application. The relocation, rental, counseling treatment plan, and wage items apply only when that expense is claimed. Application form: AK-S8 (05/2026 English) is the newest version linked from the application page and has 168 AcroForm fields; translated versions (Spanish, Tagalog, Samoan, Russian, Hmong, Simplified Chinese) are older uploads and were not saved. Address confidentiality: Alaska had no address confidentiality program until HB 239 (Chapter 9 SLA 26) enacted AS 44.21.022 in sec. 75; sec. 94 makes it effective July 1, 2026, and sec. 90 lets the Department of Administration adopt implementing regulations. The online Alaska Statutes did not yet show AS 44.21.022 when checked (Oct 3, 2026), so the rule cites the enrolled bill text. I found no Department of Administration program page, application, or enrollment regulations, so the enroll param quotes the statute's direction to adopt an enrollment procedure. Survivors of sexual assault qualify only with a protective order or by meeting other standards the department sets; people required to register under AS 12.63.010 cannot enroll; enrollment lasts five years and has no fee. Earlier bills (SB 12 in the 33rd Legislature; SB 31 and HB 104 in the 34th) stalled in finance committees. Record confidentiality: AS 18.67.030(c); the Department of Law Victims' Rights Handbook (AK-S6) says the same thing.

jurisdictions.name: Alabama

program.agency: Alabama Crime Victims Compensation Commission (ACVCC)
program.statute_citation: Ala. Code 15-23-1 to 15-23-23; Ala. Admin. Code ch. 262-X

coverage.notes: No minimum loss rule found in the statute or rules. No dollar cap found for security enhancement. No police-report alternative for sexual assault compensation claims was found; the 72-hour report rule has a good-cause exception. The exam payment program separately pays for adult 'Jane Doe' exams (r. 262-X-11-.01(4)(c)3), which suggests the exam itself does not need a police report for adults, but this is not a rule about compensation claims. For minors, the SANE facility must confirm a report to DHR or law enforcement before the exam is paid (r. 262-X-11-.01(4)(c)10). No processing time for a decision or payment is stated in the saved sources; the rules say only that approved claims are paid in order of approval as funds become available (r. 262-X-4-.04(6)). address_confidentiality: Alabama has no state address confidentiality program; the Arizona and Minnesota Secretary of State ACP directories (azsos.gov ACP_Throughout_the_United_States.pdf; sos.mn.gov Safe at Home 'Other States' page) both list 'Alabama No program', and no Alabama statute or agency page for one was found. record_confidentiality: Ala. Code 15-23-4(k) bars disclosing victim or claimant names, addresses, and crime facts; r. 262-X-2-.05 repeats this, and 15-23-5(4) makes law enforcement investigative reports received by the Commission confidential except to a grand jury.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute vs. rule on amounts: Ala. Code 15-23-15(b) sets a ceiling of $20,000 aggregate and 15-23-15(a) a $600/week ceiling for work loss; the Commission's rule (r. 262-X-4-.04, certified version effective Nov 13, 2023 on the official admin code site) sets the actual limits at $15,000 per claim and $400/week. The rule sits inside the statutory ceiling, so the rule numbers are used; the ACVCC website also says the maximum award is $15,000 (as of July 09, 2020). A July 14, 2025 notice of intended action (posted on acvcc.alabama.gov under Administrative Rule Updates) proposed raising lost wages to $500/week for up to 26 weeks ($13,000 max) and funeral to $6,000 for crimes on or after July 11, 2025; the official admin code site still showed the Nov 13, 2023 version when retrieved on 2026-10-03, so the proposal is not used. Recheck before relying on the lost-wage cap. Outstanding (unpaid) medical bills sent to providers may be paid at 30% of eligible charges up to $6,000 (r. 262-X-4-.04(3)); not modeled as a survivor-facing cap. The exam program pays providers flat fees ($400 exam without medication, $550 with medication, $300 off-base, $50 lab) per r. 262-X-11-.01(9); those are provider fee schedules, not survivor caps. The statute (15-23-121) allows providers to bill health insurance for the exam and the rule requires collateral sources first, so insurance_billing is 'allowed'. Toll-free number for victims: 1-800-541-9388 (ACVCC brochure and website footer). Statute text is from Justia (2025 Code of Alabama) because the legislature's code site is script-only. The contact, law, and admin code pages on acvcc.alabama.gov blocked automated fetches. Reviewer: the statute's 72-hour report rule is not stored as within_days because the quote says 72 hours, not days. The exam payment program pays only the initial forensic exam and STI prevention (r. 262-X-11-.01(6)); injury treatment and hospital admissions go through a regular compensation claim. How to file: the Compensation page (AL-S5) lists fax (334)290-4455, email info@acvcc.alabama.gov, and mail to P.O. Box 231267, Montgomery, Alabama 36123-1267; the application itself (AL-S8, MAR 2026, the PDF linked from the Application Form page) names email and fax, and r. 262-X-1-.01(3) also gives the PO Box and email. There is no online application; the Application Form page links to the PDF. The application PDF has 112 AcroForm fields. The ACVCC claims page (acvcc.alabama.gov/victims/claims/) blocked automated fetches on 2026-10-03, so any document checklist there was not captured. Privacy: Alabama has no address confidentiality program (no substitute-address program run by the Secretary of State or Attorney General was found; national ACP directories from the Arizona and Minnesota Secretaries of State list Alabama as having no program). Claimant identity is protected by Ala. Code 15-23-4(k) (also r. 262-X-2-.05, AL-S31), and police investigative reports the Commission receives are confidential under 15-23-5(4) (AL-S21).

jurisdictions.name: Arkansas

program.agency: Arkansas Department of Public Safety, Crime Victims Reparations Board
program.statute_citation: A.C.A. 16-90-701 to 16-90-720; forensic exams A.C.A. 12-12-401 to 12-12-404; rules 16 CAR Part 60

coverage.notes: No minimum loss appears in A.C.A. 16-90-701 to 16-90-720 or 16 CAR Part 60 (the $500 figures in 16-90-719 belong to a property-repair labor program, not a minimum loss). No per-expense cap was found for lost wages, transportation, or security, and relocation is not mentioned as covered or excluded. For compensation, the 72-hour police report rule has only a good-cause exception (16 CAR 60-203(c)(2) lists physical incapacity, mental incompetence, age, and an injury not reasonably discoverable); no sexual-assault-specific alternative such as an exam or advocate report was found. The exam statute does not say whether the survivor's insurance may be billed; 16 CAR 60-303 reduces exam payments by collateral sources, recorded as AR-EXAM-5, so insurance_billing is left 'unspecified'. Crime scene cleanup is an allowable expense in 16-90-703(1)(A)(iv), but the application (Section G) limits it to survivors or dependents of homicide victims, so it is not recorded as covered for sexual assault survivors. No official source states how long a decision or payment takes; 16 CAR 60-206(h)(2) only says the claimant is mailed notice within fifteen calendar days after the staff decision, so no processing_time rule is recorded. Arkansas has no general address confidentiality program with a substitute mailing address (the AZ SOS national ACP list calls Arkansas 'Confidentiality ONLY'); the only program is the DFA driver's license Address Confidentiality Program under A.C.A. 27-16-811, limited to domestic violence victims and dependents, recorded as AR-ACP-1 with covers_sexual_assault false. Record confidentiality under A.C.A. 16-90-711 covers only medical treatment documents and law enforcement reports already confidential under other law, not the full claim file.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Filing deadline conflict: Act 666 of 2025 (SB 430, approved 4/16/25, saved as AR-S14) changed A.C.A. 16-90-712(a)(1) from one year to five years, plus five years after age 18 for minors. The statute wins, so the rules record five years. The board's rules (16 CAR 60-203(d)(1), both the DPS January 2026 copy AR-S7 and the BLR 03/22/2026 copy AR-S13), the DPS criteria page (AR-S3), and the DPS statute compilation (AR-S6, current only through 2023) still say one year. Act 666 has no emergency clause, and I did not verify its effective date or whether it reaches older crimes, so the app should tell survivors past one year to still apply and ask the program. Statute text for 16-90-703, 712, 716 and 12-12-403 is from Justia's 2025 Arkansas Code (Act 666 itself is from the legislature's site); it matches the DPS compilation except for the 2025 change to 712. Other notes: the cooperation requirement in 16-90-712(c) does not apply to human trafficking victims or minor victims of a sex offense. 16 CAR 60-211(b)(3) lets the board waive the $2,500 counseling maximum for documented special need. 16 CAR 60-210(b)-(c) says a provider that accepts the 65% medical payment agrees not to sue the victim for the balance, and A.C.A. 16-90-720 has the board pay healthcare at the workers' compensation fee schedule. 16 CAR 60-304 sets provider reimbursement maximums for exams (facility fee, SANE nurse fee, labs, colposcope); these are provider limits, not survivor caps, and are not recorded as rules. Exam bills must reach the board within three months of the exam (16 CAR 60-302(b)), a provider obligation. 12-12-402 says no provider may require an adult victim to report in order to get treatment. The application PDF lists the board at 1 State Police Plaza Drive, Little Rock, while the DPS site lists 322 South Main Street, Suite 615; the phone 501-682-1020 is the same on both and on the OVC directory. The DPS pages name the program administrator; no person is named here. Reviewer: an advance (emergency) award must be repaid if the claimant later does not follow through with prosecution or another program requirement (16 CAR 60-207(b)(4)); the rules also require cooperation with law enforcement (60-203(f)), while the statute exempts minor victims of a sex offense from the cooperation rule (16-90-712(c)(2)). The application warns that, until the board decides, the victim/claimant is responsible to service providers for expenses (the exam is the exception under 12-12-403(c)). How to file: the DPS home page offers an online application (AR-S1) and the Documents and Forms page calls it preferred (AR-S5); the online form at crimevictims.dps.arkansas.gov is a JavaScript form whose text could not be saved, so the target URL is taken from the link on AR-S1. The paper application (AR-S8, CVRB-Application_10-6-2023.pdf, the only version linked from the DPS forms page) has no fillable AcroForm fields (0 fields), so it must be printed and filled by hand. No official source states a mailing, fax, or email submission instruction in so many words: AR-S4 says to submit the application to the reparations office and lists 322 South Main Street, Suite 615, Little Rock, AR 72201, while the application header and the Arkansas.gov portal page (AR-S15) list 1 State Police Plaza Drive, Little Rock, AR 72209 and fax 501-682-5313. I recorded mail to the DPS site address (the newer source) and no fax rule; the app should tell survivors to call 501-682-1020 to confirm where to send paper copies. The application also requires the signed Authorization to Release Information and the applicant's signature, and 16 CAR 60-206(b) requires the form be complete and come with an itemized statement and the police report or other official documentation from the reporting agency. Address confidentiality: Arkansas's only Address Confidentiality Program is a driver's license/ID program run by the DFA Office of Driver Services (A.C.A. 27-16-811, AR-S17; program page AR-S16; affidavit AR-S18). It shows a PO box on the license instead of the home address; it does not give a substitute address for other government records or forward mail. It covers victims of domestic violence and their dependents only; the statute's definition of domestic violence includes sexual abuse by a family or household member or dating partner, but not sexual assault by anyone else, so covers_sexual_assault is false. The statute and affidavit list a valid order of protection under the Domestic Abuse Act of 1991, an affidavit, and agreement to program terms; the affidavit must be imaged to the license account, which suggests enrolling at a revenue/driver services office, but no source says so in words. Record confidentiality: A.C.A. 16-90-711 (quoted from the DPS statute compilation AR-S6; same text in AR-S7) makes medical treatment documents and confidential law enforcement reports submitted with an application confidential; no source says the whole claim file or the applicant's identity is exempt from the Arkansas FOIA, and 16 CAR Part 60 has no separate confidentiality rule.

jurisdictions.name: Arizona

program.agency: Arizona Criminal Justice Commission (ACJC), Crime Victim Services; claims are processed by the County Attorney's office in the county where the crime occurred

not_found: reporting_requirement:alternatives for sexual assault (forensic exam, advocate, protective order)
coverage.notes: Arizona's caps and eligibility rules are in the administrative code (A.A.C. R10-4-101 to R10-4-111, final rules effective July 3, 2024; snapshot is Supp. 26-1, March 31, 2026), not the statute. No minimum loss is set in the rules. The rules list no relocation or home security expense; transportation for responding to a substantiated safety threat is covered under R10-4-108(C)(6)(e), and crime scene cleanup (sexual assault included) covers repairing exterior doors, locks, or windows damaged in the crime at a residence (R10-4-101(8)(b)). No statewide alternative to the 72-hour police report was found for sexual assault; the only relief is the Board's good-cause extension. A.R.S. 36-420.02 bars extra fees and balance bills to the patient for county-paid forensic exams but does not address billing the patient's insurance. The lost-wage cap has no fixed dollar amount (40 hours a week at the current minimum wage), so amount_cents is null. The ACJC program page body text sits inside a form element that the snapshot extractor drops, so no rule quotes it; the apply link (acjc.hostedbykarpel.com) comes from that page's HTML. Privacy (added Oct 3): the Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Secretary of State under A.R.S. 41-161 to 41-169 (AZ-S13). No statute, rule, or official program page was found that makes compensation claims or applicant records confidential or exempt from public records law.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Sources disagree on the filing clock: the undated ACJC brochure says to apply within two years of the crime, while A.A.C. R10-4-106(A)(7) says two years after discovery; the rule wins and is what this file uses. The application PDF linked from the ACJC page is dated June 2015 and predates the 2023/2024 rule rewrite; online filing is at acjc.hostedbykarpel.com. The program is county-run: each County Attorney's office has its own board and coordinator, and awards depend on money available to that county (R10-4-108(D)(2), (I)). A.R.S. 41-2407(E) and (F) also bar a provider who accepts program payment from billing the victim for the same service (unless the program cannot pay in full) and bar debt collection on bills included in a pending claim. Statute 13-1414 covers exams for offenses under 13-1404, 13-1405, 13-1406 and 13-3212 and dangerous crimes against children. Not used: the 2018 ACJC desk manual (predates current rules). Reviewer: the brochure also says the crime must be reported within 72 hours "of the crime"; R10-4-106(A)(4) says within 72 hours after discovery, and the rule wins. The brochure's blanket exclusion of property loss or repair is older and broader than the current rules, which pay for eyeglass/prosthetic/dental device repair (R10-4-108(C)(1)(a)(i)) and door, lock and window repair at a residence as crime scene cleanup (R10-4-101(8)(b)). R10-4-108(H)(1) requires denial for failure to cooperate with law enforcement unless the failure was due to a substantial medical, mental health, or safety risk. The forensic exam statute (A.R.S. 13-1414) covers only exam expenses arising from the need to secure evidence; follow-up medical treatment goes through the compensation claim. Filing (added Oct 3): claims go to the county program where the crime happened (A.A.C. R10-4-107(D)). Mailing addresses come from the ACJC county contact list PDF (AZ-S9), which the program page links; its 14 non-Maricopa addresses match the live program page, though several phone numbers on the PDF are older. For Maricopa the PDF lists 301 W. Jefferson, 9th Floor, but the live ACJC page and the Maricopa edition of the application (AZ-S11) say 225 West Madison Street, so the Maricopa mail rule quotes AZ-S11. The online portal (acjc.hostedbykarpel.com) is a login app that the snapshot tool cannot read, so the online rule quotes the Maricopa County Attorney page (AZ-S10), which links it for all applicants. No official source gives an email, fax, or in-person filing option. The ACJC page body (dropped by the extractor) says coordinators collect police reports, but the application and rules only ask for the report number, not a copy, so police_report is not listed as a required document. The statewide application PDF (AZ-S7, Rev. 06/2015, still the newest version) is a flat PDF with 0 AcroForm fields, and its mail-to box is a blank placeholder; the Maricopa edition is the same form with the county address filled in. Processing time is the Board's 60-day decision deadline from the rules, not a payment time. Address confidentiality (added Oct 3): the SOS eligibility page (AZ-S12) lists victims of a 'sexual offense (such as rape, sexual assault, molestation)' as eligible, plus fear for safety, a recent or planned move within Arizona to a place unknown to the perpetrator, and one piece of supporting documentation. Applications go only through a registered Application Assistant met in person (call 602-542-1653 to find one); approved participants are certified for five years and may not use the substitute address until the welcome packet and authorization card arrive. The ACP laws themselves (A.R.S. 41-161 to 41-169) were not snapshotted; the rule quotes the SOS program page. Record confidentiality: not found. A.A.C. R10-4-101 to R10-4-111 (AZ-S3) have no confidentiality section, and A.R.S. 41-2407 (AZ-S1) is silent. The application's release form (AZ-S7) says the opposite of a protection: information disclosed to the program is no longer subject to HIPAA, and the program may disclose non-identifying information for statistical purposes. County boards decide claims at open public meetings (Pinal, AZ-S14: 'The meetings are open to members of the public'; Maricopa says meeting recordings and documents are available for inspection, AZ-S10), so Tend should not tell Arizona users their claim details are confidential by law.

jurisdictions.name: California

program.agency: California Victim Compensation Board (CalVCB)
program.statute_citation: Cal. Gov. Code 13950 to 13966; Cal. Code Regs. tit. 2, 649 et seq.; Cal. Penal Code 13823.95

coverage.notes: No minimum dollar loss was found in the statute or on CalVCB pages; Gov. Code 13955(g) only requires that the injury has resulted or may result in pecuniary loss. Lost income has no separate dollar cap in the sources read (it is limited by time, generally five years, in Gov. Code 13957.5 and by the overall total). No mileage rate was found. Medical is paid at board rates (Medicare rate or 75% of billed per the What Is Covered page) rather than a fixed dollar cap. Emergency awards have no fixed dollar amount; Gov. Code 13952.5(g) ties the amount to the immediate needs of the victim, subject to board rates and limits. Whether the survivor's health insurance may be billed for the forensic exam is not addressed in Penal Code 13823.95, so insurance_billing is left unspecified. No California statute was found that makes the whole CalVCB claim file confidential or exempt from the Public Records Act; the record_confidentiality rule rests on CalVCB's own Confidentiality page (CA-S21). Gov. Code 13954 only bars the board and victim centers from disclosing documents that personally identify a minor, and that section was not saved.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text comes from Justia's 2025 California Code because leginfo.legislature.ca.gov renders section text inside form tags that the fetch tool strips; the text was cross-checked by reading the leginfo article pages directly. Gov. Code 13956, 13957, and 13957.5 each have two versions on leginfo: the version quoted here (total award $35,000, raisable to $70,000 with federal funds; relocation $3,418) and an alternate version (AB 160 of 2022 and AB 1187 of 2023) with a $100,000 total, $7,500 relocation, and no dollar cap on victim counseling that only becomes operative July 1, 2024 if General Fund money is appropriated to backfill the Restitution Fund. CalVCB's own pages (What Is Covered, FAQ) and the Benefit Reference Guide Rev. 05/2025 still state $70,000 total, $3,418 relocation, $1,000 home security, and $10,000 / 60 sessions for victim counseling, so the conditional expansion appears not to have taken effect; re-check if CalVCB publishes new limits. The total_cap rule quotes CalVCB because the statute's operative number depends on federal funding. The board may exceed the counseling and relocation caps in dire or exceptional circumstances (13957(a)(2)(C), 13957(a)(7)(E)). Penal Code 13823.95(b)(1) also says a survivor does not have to participate in the criminal justice system to get the exam. Gov. Code 13956(a)(1)(C) says committing a crime does not count as involvement when the injury resulted from rape under Penal Code 261. Gov. Code 13955(b)(1) says eligibility for non-residents victimized in California applies only while the board finds federal funds are available. The paper application listed on the CalVCB forms page is Rev. 10/2017; CalVCB also takes applications online at online.victims.ca.gov. Phone 800-777-9229 matches the OVC state directory. Reviewer: the counseling caps are recorded twice on purpose, once from the statute ($10,000, Gov. Code 13957(a)(2)(A)(i)) and once from the 2025 Benefit Reference Guide, which adds the 60-session limit for a direct victim. Gov. Code 13956(b)(1) still says an application shall be denied if the victim failed to cooperate reasonably with law enforcement, weighed against age, psychological state, and fear of retaliation; not making a police report or delaying one is not by itself grounds for denial in a sexual assault claim. Penal Code 13823.95(a) bars charging the exam to the victim 'directly or indirectly'; whether that bars billing the victim's own health insurance is not stated, so insurance_billing stays unspecified. The CalVCB FAQ says victims of crimes outside California should also file in the state where the crime occurred. How to file: the application PDF linked from the CalVCB forms page (CA-S17, Form VCGCB-VCP-005 Rev. 10/2017) is still the current English version and is fillable with 207 AcroForm fields. It says to mail the signed application to CalVCB, PO Box 3036, Sacramento, CA 95812-3036, or deliver it to a local Victim Witness Assistance Center. The online target URL https://online.victims.ca.gov/ is the link behind 'CalVCB Online' on the How To Get Compensated page (CA-S12); the visible page text names CalVCB Online but does not print the address. CA-S12 also lists fax 866-902-8669, email info@victims.ca.gov, and the same PO Box for sending bills after approval; those are for bills, not the application, so they are not recorded as submission rules. Several required_document rules come from the Benefit Reference Guide's 'Examples of What We Need' lists, which are per-expense (income loss, medical, counseling); CalVCB does not ask for a photo ID in the sources read. Processing: 'Applications can take 90 days to process' (CA-S12); qualifying emergency awards are generally paid within 30 calendar days (CA-S17). Privacy: California's address confidentiality program is Safe at Home, run by the Secretary of State (Gov. Code 6205 et seq.). The enroll text is copied from Gov. Code 6206(a) (CA-S19): applications are completed in person at a community-based victims' assistance program, with a victims' assistance counselor; 6206(a)(1)(A) lists sexual assault among the qualifying grounds. The SOS page (CA-S20) gives toll-free 877-322-5227 and SafeAtHome@sos.ca.gov, and says participants can also register as confidential voters. CalVCB's Confidentiality page (CA-S21) says claim information, including medical information, is shared only with written permission or when the law requires it, and that the signed release lets CalVCB share information with government agencies and medical, dental, mental health, and funeral providers to decide eligibility; it is an agency statement, not a statute.

jurisdictions.name: Colorado

program.agency: Colorado Department of Public Safety, Division of Criminal Justice, Office for Victims Programs (claims are decided by the crime victim compensation board in each judicial district)

coverage.notes: No statewide per-expense caps (counseling, lost wages, relocation, transportation, medical, security) were found; each judicial district board sets its own limits by policy, and the state application says some districts do not pay up to the $30,000 statutory limit. Filing deadline: after SB 24-120 (2024), C.R.S. 24-4.1-108(1)(f) only requires that the application be filed with the board and states no time limit for injury claims; property damage claims must be filed within six months (24-4.1-108(1.5)(d)), which the schema cannot express in years or days. No minimum loss amount appears in the statute. Whether insurance may be billed for the evidence-collection portion of the exam is not stated in the statute. How to file: Colorado has no single statewide submission address; the DCJ pages say to send the application to the administrator in the judicial district where the crime occurred, so the submission rule points there and the district addresses and emails are on CO-S1. The 2016 form's insurance section is information to fill in, not a separate document. Address confidentiality: Colorado's ACP is run by the Department of Personnel & Administration (Division of Central Services), not the Secretary of State; the statute (C.R.S. 24-30-2104, CO-S18) covers relocated victims of domestic violence, a sexual offense, human trafficking, or stalking. Record confidentiality: C.R.S. 24-4.1-107.5(2) makes compensation claim materials confidential, with narrow court-review and in camera exceptions.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text was taken from Justia (marked 2025), which includes the SB 24-120 amendments effective May 15, 2024; 2026 session changes, if any, were not checked. Colorado's program is decentralized: claims go to the board in the judicial district where the crime occurred, and boards may waive requirements or reduce awards (24-4.1-108(2)). The DCJ-linked state application PDF is dated 2016 and still lists a one-year filing deadline and 72-hour police notification for all claims; current statute keeps the 72-hour rule only for property damage claims (24-4.1-108(1.5)(b)) and has no deadline for injury claims, so the form's deadline was not used. Some local district pages also still state a one-year deadline; survivors should apply promptly and confirm with their district. 'Injury' includes mental impairment and pregnancy (24-4.1-102(8)). Forensic exam payment: law enforcement pays when the survivor reports; DCJ pays when the survivor does not take part (18-3-407.5); SAVE (18-3-407.7) covers related medical costs for medical and anonymous reporters, with an FY2026 cap of $4,000 per incident per the DCJ SAVE page. Phone is the OVP number listed by the federal OVC directory; local district phone numbers are on the DCJ CVC page. Reviewer (Oct 3): the SAVE page's $4,000 cap is labeled FY 2026, a fiscal year that ended June 30, 2026, so it may be stale. The state application PDF that DCJ still links (2016) states a one-year filing deadline and 72-hour police notification for all claims; current statute does not, so the app should warn users that the form's eligibility text is outdated. The phone listed is the OVP main line from the OVC directory; the DCJ how-to-file page also gives a separate number for help finding the right district administrator. How-to-file pass (Oct 3): the state application CO-S13 (2016) is still the version DCJ links from both the How to File page and the Spanish section; no newer statewide PDF was linked, so it is the application_form (fillable, 152 AcroForm fields). Submission is decentralized: one mail rule targets 'the appropriate administrator' from the DCJ page; the per-district addresses on CO-S1 were not turned into separate rules because each sits next to a named contact person. The DCJ page also gives (720) 672-2166 and a staff email for help finding the right administrator, which is a help line, not a submission target. Processing time: DCJ says generally 30-45 days to a decision and that it varies by district; the 2016 form says the investigation may take up to 60 days. Privacy pass (Oct 3): ACP enrollment goes only through a certified Application Assistant at a victim-services agency; the enroll page also says applicants must have relocated within the past 90 days or plan to relocate, must reside in Colorado, and must provide documentation of eligibility (for example police reports, protection orders, or a letter from a counselor or advocate). Certification lasts 4 years. The DCS site posted a notice on Sept. 28, 2026 that it is migrating during October 2026, so the ACP URLs may change. C.R.S. 24-4.1-107.5 (CO-S15) also bars boards from producing claim records through discovery except for court review of a board decision or on a strict showing that the information exists only in board records, after in camera review and a court finding that release will not threaten the victim's safety.

jurisdictions.name: Connecticut

program.agency: State of Connecticut Judicial Branch, Office of Victim Services
program.statute_citation: Conn. Gen. Stat. 54-201 to 54-218

coverage.notes: No minimum loss appears in the statute. Sec. 54-217 now allows only expedited processing of a claim for undue hardship; its history note says older versions set an emergency award amount, but the current text sets none, so emergency_award is left out. No relocation benefit appears in the statute, brochure, benefits chart or application. No separate cap on counseling, lost wages, medical or court travel was found beyond the overall caps; the $5,000 cap (CT-CAP-2) applies only to emotional-harm-only claims. The statute sets no number of days for the police report, though the application asks whether the crime was reported within 5 days. Sec. 54-207 (regulations) is repealed and sec. 54-207a delegates procedures to the Chief Court Administrator; no administrative rules setting caps were found. The program web pages on jud.ct.gov (compensation.htm, safe.htm, svc_providers.htm) could not be saved because the fetch tool strips the page-wide form element those pages use, so the brochure, application and benefits chart PDFs stand in for them. No processing time for a decision or payment is stated in the application, brochure, benefits chart or statute.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is from the Connecticut General Assembly's current chapter pages. Exam billing: sec. 19a-112a(e)(1) bars charging exam costs directly or indirectly to the survivor and routes them to the Forensic Sex Evidence Exams account; it does not expressly mention billing the survivor's insurance, so insurance_billing is 'unspecified'. The OVS SAFE page (https://www.jud.ct.gov/crimevictim/safe.htm, not saveable with the tool) says a patient cannot receive a bill for the exam and tells patients to call OVS at 1-800-822-8428 if they or their insurer get a bill. Caps: sec. 54-211(d)(2) allows up to $5,000 more for minors with extra medical or counseling needs and (d)(3) allows going over the caps for good cause; these are not encoded as rules. The $1,000 crime scene cleanup and security cap comes from program documents, not the statute. Under sec. 54-212 OVS may recover two-thirds of what it paid from later recoveries; not encoded. The program phone 1-888-286-7347 is from the brochure; the OVS general line on the federal OVC directory is 860-263-2760. Reviewer check (Oct 3): the 2026 Supplement on cga.ct.gov amends only secs. 54-203 and 54-230 in chapter 968, and its version of 19a-112a(e) (amended by P.A. 25-29) is word for word the same as the saved text, so the caps, deadline, reporting and exam rules above are current through the 2025 session. Acts from the 2026 session were not checked. 'Emotional harm' in sec. 54-201(6) means impairment from a threat of physical injury or death, so the $5,000 cap (CT-CAP-2) is for threat-only claims; sexual assault involving actual bodily harm falls under the $15,000 cap. CT-CAP-3, CT-CAP-4 and CT-CAP-5 are one shared $1,000 benefit, not three. 'Charged directly or indirectly to such victim' in 19a-112a(e) may reach insurance billing, but the statute does not say so, so insurance_billing stays 'unspecified'. How to file (Oct 3): the application JD-VS-8PI (Rev. 7/21, CT-S4) is still the version served at program.application_pdf_url (same sha256 on re-download) and has 296 AcroForm fields. It lists mail, fax and email as the ways to send it; no online filing portal or in-person drop-off is stated in the saved sources, and compensation.htm still could not be saved (blocked or empty even through Chrome). The application asks for the police report number but not a copy of the report, so no police_report document rule was added. The application must carry a handwritten signature. Privacy (Oct 3): the Address Confidentiality Program is in chapter 968a (secs. 54-240 to 54-240o, CT-S9) and run by the Secretary of the State; sec. 54-240a(a) and 54-240c list sexual assault as a qualifying crime, and sec. 54-240b(a) says each application must be completed with an application assistant. The SOTS page (CT-S10) says applications may only be submitted by application assistants tied to a domestic violence or sexual assault advocacy organization. Record confidentiality is narrow: sec. 54-204(b) only keeps information that is already confidential under other statutes confidential while OVS or a commissioner holds it; no statute found in chapter 968 that makes the compensation claim file itself exempt from public disclosure. Secs. 54-228 and 54-230 separately keep a victim's notification request and mailing address confidential, but those cover offender-release notification, not compensation claims.

jurisdictions.name: District of Columbia

program.agency: Superior Court of the District of Columbia
program.statute_citation: D.C. Code §§ 4-501 to 4-518; D.C. Super. Ct. CVCP Rules; D.C. Code §§ 4-561.03 and 23-1908 (PERK)

coverage.notes: D.C. Code 4-506(d) lets the program waive its time limits for good cause, including compelling health or safety concerns (not encoded as a separate deadline rule). No minimum-loss threshold appears in D.C. Code 4-501 to 4-512 or the CVCP Rules. D.C. Code 4-561.03 bars the hospital from billing the survivor for a PERK, but no official source I saved names who pays the hospital or says whether the survivor's private insurance may be billed, so exam_payment is left out and insurance_billing is unspecified. Processing time: the 2023 application asks applicants to allow 5 business days for staff review of the application; no official source states a time to a decision or payment. Address confidentiality: D.C.'s ACP (Address Confidentiality Act of 2018, D.C. Law 22-118) is run by OVSJG; the OVSJG ACP page (DC-S18) lists sexual assault among qualifying experiences. Record confidentiality: D.C. Code 4-511 (DC-S17) makes claim files confidential and not open to public inspection.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Dollar sub-limits come from the D.C. Superior Court CVCP Rules (DC-S7); the statute (4-501(7)) lists covered costs but sets only the $10,000 funeral cap and the $25,000 total. The Rules PDF is older than the 2023 amendments (D.C. Law 24-341) in places: Rule 25 says funeral up to $6,000, while statute 4-501(7)(A)(ii), the program's Compensable Costs page, and the 2023 application all say $10,000 (statute wins). Rule 7(b) lists only a sexual assault exam as the reporting alternative; statute 4-506(c)(3) is broader (protective order, forensic exam, or a report before the statute of limitations), and the statute is used here. The Application page (DC-S4) says to submit a DC police report or DC civil protection order and that temporary restraining orders are not accepted, while the 2023 application form (DC-S6) lists forensic medical examination as crime documentation; Tend should follow the statute and tell survivors to call the program if documentation is questioned. 4-506(a-2) also says arrest, prosecution, or conviction of the offender is not required, and being a family or household member of the offender does not by itself make a claimant ineligible. Federal OVC directory confirmed the program website and phone 202-879-4216. Reviewer pass: added the statutory $10,000 funeral cap (4-501(7)(A)(ii)) as its own rule, the $2,500 per-victimization limit on loss of services alongside the $200 weekly limit, and the 4-508(b)(2) law-enforcement cooperation ground for denial. Rule 33 covers only a rental car, while the 2023 statute covers alternate transportation including rideshare; the $2,000 figure comes from the Rules, the Compensable Costs page, and the 2023 application. The CVCP Rules PDF carries no adoption date; its dollar sub-limits other than funeral match the current Compensable Costs page and the 2023 application form. No official source found names who pays the hospital for the PERK exam. How to file: the 2023 application (DC-S6, 443 AcroForm fields, the version linked from the program's Application page) says to submit by email to CVCPapplications@dcsc.gov or by mail or in person at 515 5th Street, NW #109, or at remote sites; the brochure (DC-S5) lists five Balance and Restorative Justice Center remote sites for pick-up and drop-off. The Application page (DC-S4) adds fax 202-879-4230 and shows the email address obfuscated, so the email rule quotes the application form. D.C. Code 4-512(a) confirms filing in person, by mail, online, or by email. The online target comes from the brochure, where a PDF line break splits the URL ('Gene rateInterview'); the joined URL is the same link the D.C. Courts Forms Help Online page (DC-S16) uses for its Start Your Online Interview button and it returned HTTP 200 on Oct 3. The application asks for a photo ID but says staff will confirm identity another way if none is attached. Address confidentiality: the OVSJG ACP page (DC-S18) says an applicant may qualify if they fear for their safety, currently (or will soon) reside in D.C., and have experienced domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or human trafficking; they must also have moved within the past 60 days, plan to move within 30 days, or have kept their current address off online and public records. The substitute address binds District agencies only; the page says non-government entities may still require the actual address and the program does not forward packages or magazines. The program is created by D.C. Law 22-118 (Address Confidentiality Act of 2018); the statute itself was not saved, so the rule quotes the official program page. Record confidentiality: D.C. Code 4-511(a) (DC-S17) is the statute; CVCP Rule 4 (DC-S7) and the Application page (DC-S4) say the same thing. 4-511(a) lets the claimant, an authorized representative, physicians at the Court's discretion, and people assisting the Court see the file, and 4-507(f) lets the Court tell the sentencing judge the award amount, so Tend should not say no one outside the program ever sees the claim.

jurisdictions.name: Delaware

program.agency: Delaware Department of Justice

not_found: expense_cap:counseling (no general adult counseling cap found; see notes)
covered_expense:transportation (no general transportation benefit found outside ambulance transport within the forensic exam and court-attendance expenses)
expense_cap:medical (no dollar cap; regulations set payment at 80% of usual and customary charges)
coverage.notes: Statute text is from the official Delaware Code Online. Counseling: the only counseling limits found are $1,200 per child victim for psychological assessment and short-term counseling under the Child Victim Counseling and Assessment Program (1 Del. Admin. Code 301-26.0, 11 Del. C. § 9024) and a 50-session limit that applies only to reopened claims under § 9009(13); neither is encoded as a general counseling cap. Medical, mental health, and dental providers paid by VCAP must accept the VCAP payment as payment in full and may not bill the victim the balance (Rules 28.1, 29.1, 30.1); VCAP pays 80% of usual and customary charges (Rules 28.2, 29.2, 30.2). The printable application PDF is an image scan with no extractable text, so no rules were drawn from it. No separate SANE or forensic exam payment policy beyond 11 Del. C. § 9023 was located.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Sources disagree in a few places and the statute controls: (1) the regulation sets the funeral and burial cap at $5,000 (Rule 25.0) while 11 Del. C. § 9002(10)s. sets $7,500; funeral is not encoded. (2) The program FAQ states the 72-hour police report requirement without exceptions, but § 9010(a)(5) waives it for, among other things, a protection from abuse order or cooperation with law enforcement or an appropriate government agency in sexual assault cases. (3) Rule 13.2 says reconsideration must be requested within 15 days; § 9012(b) says 30 days. (4) The statute measures the filing deadline from the personal injury and Rule 11.1 from the date of the crime; for sexual assault these are normally the same day. Additional sexual-assault-specific provisions: § 9009(11) lets a victim of a crime that occurred before age 18 claim counseling up to the 20th birthday, and that age limit does not apply to sexual assault or abuse; § 9009(12) bars statute of limitations limits on claims from child sexual assault or abuse; § 9010(d) bars denial solely because a child sexual assault victim delayed reporting or applying. Forensic exam payment flows provider to insurance to the fund under § 9023, so insurance_billing is recorded as allowed (the provider must bill insurance) while the survivor owes nothing out of pocket. Reviewer: the brochure lists attorneys fees as not eligible, but 11 Del. C. § 9013 and Rule 19.0 let the Appeals Board award fees for representation before it (up to $1,000 or 15% of the award, whichever is less, in addition to compensation); the statute controls, so the brochure exclusion was replaced by that cap (DE-CAP-6). Housing-related costs (rent, security deposit, furniture) under § 9002(10)h. are capped at 3 times the monthly prospective housing cost, which is not a fixed dollar amount and so is not encoded. Rule 27.1 says life insurance proceeds are not deducted from the award. Filing info (added Oct 3): the brochure lists mail, fax, and online (https://ccvcde.org) as the ways to submit a claim. Email (VCAP@delaware.gov) appears only as contact info, not as a filing method, so no email submission rule was added. The brochure mailing address reads '900 N. King Street, 4th Floor' while the DOJ page, the online portal (DE-S6), and the claim form header read '900 North King St., Suite 4', both Wilmington, DE 19801; the brochure is the only text source that names it as the place to mail claims, so it is encoded as written and the reviewer may want to confirm. The printable application (DE-S4, title 'DE VCAP CLAIM FORM 12-09', footer 'VCAP Claim Form (1/10)') is a 3-page image scan with no text layer and no AcroForm fields, so nothing is quoted from it; visually it says 'Complete and submit to' the Suite 4 address, asks the applicant to attach any medical bills received, lists the police complaint number, and requires the claimant's signature to be witnessed by an adult over 18 plus a signed HIPAA authorization. Those form items are not encoded because they cannot be verified against extracted text. Processing time comes from the brochure (up to 60 days for a decision); 11 Del. C. § 9012(a) separately says the Agency starts its investigation within 30 days of filing. Privacy (added Oct 3): Delaware's Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Department of Justice, not the Secretary of State (11 Del. C. § 9611(6), § 9612(a): 'Upon application and certification, persons eligible pursuant to this subchapter shall be provided a substitute address by the Program.'). Sexual assault victims qualify under § 9613(1) only if they have filed for a protection from abuse order or are named as a victim in a criminal or delinquency proceeding, and they must also state that they fear future violent acts by the perpetrator; § 9611(15) defines victim of sexual assault by reference to §§ 768 through 780 and 787. Certification lasts 3 years (§ 9614). ACP application records and actual addresses are confidential and exempt from FOIA (§ 9612(d)). The statute leaves the application method to the Program, and no official DOJ page describing the application steps was found; the DOJ Criminal Division page gives only the contact DOJ_ACP@delaware.gov. Record confidentiality: 29 Del. C. § 10002(o)(14) excludes VCAP investigative files from public records. VCAP Rule 12.0 says VCAP, the Advisory Council, and the Appeals Board shall maintain confidentiality of records under FOIA, and Rule 9.4 governs public access to crime victims' case files under FOIA; both rules cite older FOIA subsection letters (§10002(g)(14) and §1004(g)(7)) that now correspond to § 10002(o)(14). Under § 10004(h)(8) the VCAP Appeals Board may close a meeting when the claim derives from a sexual offense.

jurisdictions.name: Florida

program.agency: Office of the Attorney General (Department of Legal Affairs), Division of Victim Services and Criminal Justice Programs, Bureau of Victim Compensation
program.statute_citation: Fla. Stat. 960.01 to 960.28; Fla. Admin. Code R. 2A-2.2001 to 2A-2.2003

coverage.notes: No minimum dollar loss exists; instead Fla. Stat. 960.13(8) says the department shall deny an award if the claimant will not suffer serious financial hardship, considering all the claimant's financial resources. No transportation cap and no security or lock-replacement expense were found in the statute, rules, or program publications. No alternative to a police report was found for compensation claims: Fla. Admin. Code R. 2A-2.2001(9)-(10) limit proof of crime to law enforcement and prosecutors (including form BVC430). The separate forensic exam payment under 960.28 does not require reporting or cooperation. Phones and other personal property: Florida reimburses tangible property loss only through the Property Loss program for elderly persons or disabled adults (960.195); R. 2A-2.2002(3)(f) lists a telephone as an example of compensable property for that program. A typical adult survivor under the elderly or disabled criteria has no property benefit. 960.28 says the forensic exam is paid regardless of insurance and the victim may not be required to pay directly or indirectly, but it does not say whether the provider may bill the victim's insurer, so insurance_billing is 'unspecified'. No official source found states a processing time for a decision or payment. Address confidentiality: Florida's ACP (Fla. Stat. 741.401-741.465, run by the Attorney General) is limited to victims of domestic violence and dating violence (741.403(1)(a)), extended to victims of stalking or aggravated stalking by 741.4651. A sexual assault or sexual battery survivor qualifies only when the act counts as domestic violence or dating violence (741.402(2) lists sexual assault and sexual battery within dating violence when committed by a romantic or intimate partner), so covers_sexual_assault is false.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute vs rule: 960.13(9)(a) sets a $25,000 total ceiling and $10,000 for treatment, but 960.13(9)(b) lets the department set lower limits by rule, and R. 2A-2.2003 (Schedule of Benefits) caps a living, non-catastrophic victim at $15,000 per claim. I used the rule/schedule figures because they are what the program applies; both are consistent. Schedule caps are taken from the official Schedule of Benefits PDF (FL-S16) because the Cornell LII copy of R. 2A-2.2003 (FL-S12) prints dollar amounts as '$15, 000.00', which breaks number matching; the amounts are identical. Provider payments for medical and mental health are at a rate of 50% or less depending on funds, while victim out-of-pocket reimbursement is at 100 percent (R. 2A-2.2002(2)(e)2.). Older crimes (before October 1, 2019) have a 72-hour reporting rule and 1-year filing deadline (2 years with good cause); the rules here cover crimes on or after that date. The brochure and claim form state reporting within 120 hours, matching the statutory five days. Domestic violence relocation discrepancy: Fla. Stat. 960.198 (amended by ch. 2026-86) now allows up to $2,500 per claim and $5,000 lifetime, while R. 2A-2.2003 and the Schedule of Benefits still list $1,500 and $3,000. Statute governs; not encoded as a rule because it is DV-specific. Sexual battery relocation (960.199) matches the rule at $1,500 and $3,000. Relocation assistance types (DV, sexual battery, human trafficking) are mutually exclusive for the same incident. LII copies of R. 2A-2.2001 and 2A-2.2002 were cross-checked against the current Word versions on flrules.org for every quoted passage. Medical providers must submit the forensic exam claim (BVC100SB) within 120 days of the exam; this binds providers, not survivors. Reviewer additions: The Schedule of Benefits caps (FL-S16) apply to crimes on or after January 6, 2022; the program page links a separate schedule for earlier crime dates, and the LII notes say the rule amendment took effect 1/9/2022. FL-CAP-8 quotes the Schedule PDF, whose two-column text extraction puts the $10,000 figure for the 'Minor Victim Mental Injury' row ahead of the $5,000 figure for the 'Adult or Minor Victim of Forcible Felony (non injury)' row; the LII copy of R. 2A-2.2003 (FL-S12) lists the rows in order and confirms $5,000 at 50%, one year, for the non-injury forcible felony row. FL-DEADLINE-3 is the good-cause extension ceiling (5 years), not the base deadline; the base deadline is FL-DEADLINE-1 (3 years). Compensation also requires cooperation with law enforcement and the state attorney (960.13(1)(b)), which the department can use to deny, reduce, or withdraw an award; the separate forensic exam payment does not. For minors, 960.07(3) says good cause can extend the paragraph (c) period 'for an additional period not to exceed 2 years', and kit testing or DNA matching delays can waive any filing deadline; this is described in FL-DEADLINE-2's extension text rather than quoted, to keep the quote short. How to file (added Oct 3): the claim form BVC100 (08/24), saved as FL-S18 and still the form linked from the program page, has 138 fillable AcroForm fields. Section One, instruction 4 says to submit the application and documents via email, fax, or mail; the address, email, and fax come from the form's page 1 header. Fla. Stat. 960.07(5) also allows filing in person at the Tallahassee office. No online method is encoded: the VANext portal is described on the program page and brochure as for advocates and providers (the brochure says victim service practitioners can register for access to the online claims submission portal), not survivors. The FL-S18 text extraction drops the 'ti', 'tt', and 'ft' ligatures (for example 'applica on', 'A ach'), so quotes from that source keep those gaps to stay verbatim; the brochure (FL-S17) is used where it states the same requirement in clean text. Privacy protections (added Oct 3): FL-ACP-1 quotes the Attorney General's ACP page, which the Bureau of Criminal Justice Programs page links to on fcpti.com (the AG's Florida Crime Prevention Training Institute site); no ACP page exists on myfloridalegal.com. The enroll text combines the page's switchboard instruction with 741.403(2) (FL-S20): 'Applications must be filed with the Office of the Attorney General. An application fee may not be charged.' Certification lasts 4 years (741.403(3)). The statute's full program name is 'Address Confidentiality Program for Victims of Domestic and Dating Violence' (741.4651, FL-S22). covers_sexual_assault is false because no quote makes sexual assault survivors eligible as such: 741.403(1)(a) requires a sworn statement that the applicant is a victim of domestic violence or dating violence, and 741.402(2) (FL-S24) defines dating violence to include sexual assault and sexual battery only when committed by someone with a romantic or intimate relationship with the victim; stalking victims are added by 741.4651. A survivor of non-partner sexual assault who is also being stalked may qualify through 741.4651. Record confidentiality: FL-RECORDS-1 relies on Fla. Stat. 119.071(2)(j)1.b.(I), which exempts victim-identifying information in records of any agency that regularly receives information concerning crime victims; the quote does not name the compensation bureau, but the bureau is such an agency. The compensation chapter itself has only Fla. Stat. 960.15 (FL-S21): 'Any record or report obtained by the department or a hearing officer that is confidential or exempt from the provisions of s. 119.07 (1) shall retain that status and shall not be subject to public disclosure.' That keeps already-confidential records (for example medical records) confidential but does not make the whole claim file confidential. Separately, 119.071(2)(h)1.b. makes information that may reveal the identity of a victim of any sexual offense confidential and exempt, but only within criminal intelligence or investigative information. 119.071(2)(j)1.b. is set to sunset on October 2, 2031 unless reenacted, reverting to a narrower 'any document' exemption with similar coverage. No official program statement on confidentiality was found in the brochure, claim form, or program page.

jurisdictions.name: Georgia

program.agency: Criminal Justice Coordinating Council (CJCC), Victims Compensation Division
program.statute_citation: O.C.G.A. 17-15-1 to 17-15-17; forensic exam: O.C.G.A. 17-5-72 and 17-15-15; rules: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 144-4-.06 and 144-4-.08

coverage.notes: Georgia's statute and program pages list only medical/dental, lost wages, loss of support, funeral, counseling and crime scene sanitization as benefit categories. I found no source covering relocation, transportation, security, or temporary housing, and no source that expressly excludes them, so they are left as not found rather than marked excluded. No minimum loss amount and no emergency or advance award provision appear in O.C.G.A. 17-15 (section list checked) or the CJCC rules. Toll-free number 800-547-0060 is also listed on the application. The 1-year filing rule applies to crimes before July 1, 2014 (per the CJCC program page); the 3-year rule in O.C.G.A. 17-15-5 applies to later crimes. Filing: the application (Revised Sept 2026) names mail and the online portal as the two ways to file; it lists a fax number, (404) 463-7652, as contact information but does not say applications can be faxed, so no fax, email, or in-person submission rule was added. The only stated time is for payment after an award (up to eight weeks); no official source states how long a decision takes for a victim claim (the FAQ's under-30-days figure is for provider FME applications).

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is from Justia's 2025 Georgia Code because Georgia does not host an official free O.C.G.A. text; the CJCC pages cite the same section. The CJCC 'What Our Programs Cover' page (GA-S6) shows one combined line, 'Loss of Income or Support Up to $20,000'; this reads as the two separate $10,000 statutory categories (lost wages and loss of support, O.C.G.A. 17-15-8(c)(2), also GA-S7, GA-S10, GA-S11) added together, so the lost wages cap is $10,000. Police report: the statute's 72-hour rule (O.C.G.A. 17-15-8(a)(3)) has a good cause exception, and the CJCC FAQ says sexual assaults after May 12, 2008 need no police report because exam documentation can be used; I did not find the statutory text behind the FAQ statement, so GA-REPORT-2 rests on the official FAQ. Counseling: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 144-4-.06(8)(a) requires a Psychological Service Report after the first visit, while GA-S6 says it is required beyond the fourth session. The forensic exam is paid by a separate CJCC Forensic Medical Examination Program (providers apply directly), not out of the survivor's $25,000 compensation award. The CJCC landing page and the 'How the Application Review Process Works' page could not be saved (the fetcher flagged them as blocked or empty). Reviewer additions: the $1,000 exam payment is a per-victimization total across all providers; if bills exceed it, the program splits $1,000 among providers (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 144-4-.08(2)(e)), and the FAQ calls the $1,000 the maximum for 'the collection of evidence for a FME'. The statutory FME definition (O.C.G.A. 17-15-2(6)) includes testing needed to collect evidence and provide treatment, but other follow-up medical care goes through the regular compensation claim. O.C.G.A. 17-15-8(a)(3) presumes good cause for a late report for trafficking victims under 17-15-7(a)(1)(D). The CJCC program page and the application still list a police or incident report as part of a Complete Application Packet; the application also says an applicant may submit without one and the program will follow up. The 72-hour reporting rule is not tied to sexual assault in the statute; only the FAQ (GA-S3) carves out sexual assault, so treat GA-REPORT-2 as program practice, not statute. Packet step additions: the application PDF (GA-S10, Revised September 2026, newest on the CJCC forms page) is a flat, non-fillable PDF with 0 AcroForm fields, so it must be printed and filled by hand or the survivor can apply through the portal. GA-S7 also gives the mailing address as 'Georgia Crime Victims Compensation at 104 Marietta Street NW, Suite 400 Atlanta, GA 30303'; the rule uses the application's fuller addressee. The application says a signed application can be submitted without all documents (such as a police report) and the program will follow up. Lost wages documents come from the CJCC lost wages enclosure (GA-S21, Rev. 06/28/19); the employer's verification form (GA-S20) must be faxed or mailed by the employer, not the survivor. GA-S19 lists what an investigative report must contain (names, dates, summary, injuries) and is saved for reference. Privacy additions: Georgia's address confidentiality program is Safe at Home, run by the Secretary of State under O.C.G.A. 50-18-150 to 50-18-155 (SB 324), which took effect and began accepting applications July 1, 2026. The SOS page (GA-S22) lists sexual assault survivors as eligible, and O.C.G.A. 50-18-151(b) (GA-S23) lets an applicant qualify by affidavit that they have been a victim of sexual assault, among other offenses. The statute also requires a letter from a victim advocate or provider showing the applicant received services related to their victimization (50-18-151(c)(7)), so enrollment is not just the sworn application; it makes the application and participant information confidential and not a public record (50-18-151(g)); certification lasts four years. Record confidentiality: I found no Georgia statute or rule that makes the compensation claim file itself confidential or exempt from the Open Records Act. What exists is O.C.G.A. 17-15-4(a)(2) (GA-S24), which requires the board to preserve the confidentiality of records it receives from other agencies, and O.C.G.A. 17-15-6(c) (GA-S25), which excludes information deemed confidential from an investigative report given to the claimant. The CJCC medical release form also says the program will preserve the confidentiality of all records received, but I did not save it. Treat GA-RECCONF-1 as narrow: it covers records the board collects, not a blanket confidentiality rule for applications.

jurisdictions.name: Hawaii

program.agency: Hawaii Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, Crime Victim Compensation Commission
program.statute_citation: Haw. Rev. Stat. ch. 351; Haw. Admin. R. ch. 23-605

not_found: reporting alternatives for sexual assault (forensic exam, advocate, protective order)
coverage.notes: No Hawaii statute was found that says who pays for a sexual assault forensic exam or whether insurance may be billed; the only official statement found is the Attorney General HSART program page saying police are to ensure free exams regardless of reporting. No per-expense caps, minimum loss, or emergency award were found in HRS ch. 351 or HAR ch. 23-605; HAR 23-605-15 says administrative award guidelines may be set by the commission, but none were found published. No police-report alternative for sexual assault was found: HRS 351-31(d) requires an arrest or a police report without undue delay (72 hours under HAR 23-605-2, with a good cause exception). The 18 month filing deadline is stored as params.months because the schema has only years or days. No statute, rule, or official program statement was found that makes Crime Victim Compensation Commission records, claims, or applicant information confidential: HRS ch. 351 and HAR ch. 23-605 as saved contain no such provision, and the CVCC pages and application form do not state one.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is from capitol.hawaii.gov (HRS current). HAR ch. 23-605 is an OCR'd 2001 PDF hosted by the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation; quotes were taken only from clean stretches, and garbled passages (the four-day lost earnings limit without a medical certificate in 23-605-12(c), and the therapy exclusions in 23-605-10(c)) were left out. HAR 23-605-6(a) limits out-of-state claims by Hawaii residents to states without an eligible compensation program, which HRS 351-31(a) does not say; the statute was used. The CVCC brochure PDF (Compensation_Brochure_2026c.pdf) extracts as font-encoded garbage, so it was not saved or quoted; its deadline sentence could not be read. The $10,000 cap in HRS 351-62(b) is the current statute text as retrieved; the medical-expense exception raises it to at most $20,000. The Acknowledgement Award on the CVCC page cites HRS 351-33(4) (pain and suffering). The Sex Abuse Treatment Center (a Hawaii Pacific Health program, not a state agency) states its medical forensic exam is free; it was not used as a rule source. Reviewer (Oct 3): HI-EXAM-1 rests only on the AG HSART page's description of the police role; a search and a check of Act 113 (2018) and HRS 844D-24 found no Hawaii statute saying who pays for the forensic exam or barring bills to the victim or insurer. The 18 month deadline is stored as params.months (not a schema key); the engine must read it. The 72 hour police-report window is stored without within_days because the source states hours, not days. HAR 23-605-12(c) appears to limit lost earnings to four days without a medical certificate, but the OCR is garbled so it is not quoted. How to file (Oct 3): the How to Apply page (HI-S3) says to mail or drop off the signed application at 1164 Bishop St, Suite 1530, Honolulu; the June 2026 fillable English application (HI-S7, still the form linked from that page, 112 AcroForm fields) also lists a fax number and email under 'SUBMIT THE ORIGINALLY SIGNED APPLICATION TO'. HAR 23-605-4(b) says an original signed application must also be submitted when documents are sent electronically, so fax and email do not replace the signed original. No online portal was found. The Commission requests the police report itself, so it is stored as a police_report rule with a note that it does not go in the packet. No processing time is stated: the FAQ (HI-S4) says only that case processing time varies. The supporting documents list on HI-S3 says 'bills', not itemized bills; it is stored as itemized_bill with that note. Privacy (Oct 3): Hawaii's Address Confidentiality Program is established by HRS ch. 801G (Act 115, 2018) in the Department of Law Enforcement (HRS 801G-1 defines "Department" as the department of law enforcement; HRS 801G-2(a) says the program protects the actual address of a victim of domestic abuse, a sexual offense, or stalking and assigns a substitute address used by agencies). HRS 801G-1 defines "sexual offense" by listing Penal Code sections and makes a victim of a sexual offense a primary applicant. HRS 801G-3(a) requires a primary applicant to be assisted by an application assistant, matching the DLE page. The DLE page also lists HAR ch. 24-1000, which was not saved. record_confidentiality: none found. An Office of Information Practices opinion letter (Op. Ltr. 03-02, files.hawaii.gov/oip) addressed CVCC records under the UIPA (HRS ch. 92F): it says the Commission may withhold applicant information whose disclosure would be a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy or would frustrate its function, and it was partially overruled by Op. Ltr. 05-03 to the extent it implied the privacy exception mandates confidentiality. That letter is an opinion, not a statute or program statement, and it does not make the records confidential, so it was not saved or used as a rule.

jurisdictions.name: Iowa

program.agency: Iowa Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General, Crime Victim Assistance Division (Victim Assistance Section)
program.statute_citation: Iowa Code 915.80 to 915.94; Iowa Code 915.41 (exam costs); Iowa Admin. Code 61, ch. 9

coverage.notes: Iowa sets per-category limits in Iowa Code 915.86 and no overall maximum award was found in the statute, rules, or program pages, so total_cap is left out. No minimum out-of-pocket loss was found. Housing assistance (915.86(17)) is in the statute but the program facts page lists it as currently unavailable. Address confidentiality: Iowa's Safe at Home program (Iowa Code chapter 9E, IA-S11) is run by the Secretary of State; the program page (IA-S13) lists survivors of sexual assault and 9E.1 and 9E.2 name sexual abuse victims as eligible. Record confidentiality: Iowa Code 915.90 keeps confidential records the program receives confidential; no statute making the whole claim file exempt from public records was found.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is the Iowa Code 2026 chapter 915 PDF from legis.iowa.gov; rules are 61 IAC ch. 9 (IAC 2/5/25, ARC 8358C effective 12/18/24). Exam payment: 61 IAC 9.83(2) pays qualified providers a $400 provider fee plus a $300 facility fee for exams within 30 days; the exam program has no application for the survivor. Survivor-relevant extras not encoded as rules: 61 IAC 9.30(4) says a sexual abuse victim is deemed to have reasonably cooperated with law enforcement if the victim undergoes a sexual abuse evidentiary examination; Iowa Code 915.84(4) exempts certain child and dependent adult sexual abuse victims from police reporting when the abuse was reported to and verified by HHS; the quick guide says criminal charges do not have to be filed. 61 IAC 9.35(3) pays up to 12 counseling sessions in full with a treatment plan, after which preexisting issues can reduce payment; this is not a hard session cap, so it is not encoded as count_limit. Iowa Code 915.86(18) allows up to $5,000 per person of additional compensation for undue hardship or new events beyond category limits (not for relocation, housing, or loss of support); not encoded. The program facts page and 61 IAC 9.35(8) say lost wages beyond two weeks need a disability statement. Phones and other personal property: not covered (property loss excluded), but medical devices and medication taken, lost, or destroyed in the crime can be replaced under 61 IAC 9.35(1)(g). The Capitol program phone 515-281-5044 also appears on the exam page (IA-S3). Facts page IA-S2 contains the same quick facts as program page IA-S1. Reviewer: Iowa Code 915.84(2) lets the department waive the 30-day emergency relocation window for good cause. Iowa Code 915.86(1)(b) says a medical provider that accepts the program's full payment at the established rate must hold the victim harmless for the rest. IA-COUNS-2 ($2,000) and IA-WAGES-2 ($1,000) are caps for secondary victims and for court or investigation time, not the primary victim's main counseling or lost-wage caps (IA-COUNS-1, IA-WAGES-1). Housing assistance (IA-HOUSING-1) has no matching benefit category in 61 IAC 9.35 and the facts page says it is currently unavailable, so treat it as not currently paid. How to file (added Oct 3): the English primary victim application (IA-S5, 2023 brochure, PDF dated Aug 15 2023) is still the one linked from the program and printable-applications pages; it is a flat print-and-sign PDF with no form fields. The online application page (IA-S8) links to the portal at ccvcia.org (IA-S10), where you must create an account to file. Mailing address conflict: the 2023 brochure's contact panel lists the Lucas State Office Building, Ground Floor, 321 East 12th Street, and its business reply panel is addressed to the State Capitol, 1015 E Grand Ave, Des Moines IA 50319-9903; the current portal and every AG page list the Hoover Building, 1305 E Walnut Street, so IA-SUBMIT-2 uses Hoover. No source says the application can be faxed or emailed: fax 515-281-8199 appears only as a contact number and crimevictiminfo@ag.iowa.gov only 'for help', so neither is encoded as a submission method. Filing by phone at 1-800-373-5044 is allowed (61 IAC 9.28, facts page) but phone is not a schema submission method. No source asks the applicant to attach a police report; the application asks for the law enforcement agency and case number instead, and 61 IAC 9.33 refers to a law enforcement verification form the program sends to police. Privacy (added Oct 3): Safe at Home, Iowa Code chapter 9E (IA-S11), run by the Secretary of State. Iowa Code 9E.2(6)(a)(1) makes eligible a victim of sexual abuse as evidenced by a petition under 236.3 or a criminal complaint or information under 708.1, 708.2A, 708.11, 710A.2, or any chapter 709 violation, but 9E.3(1)(b)(1) lets the applicant instead state good reason to believe the person is a victim of sexual abuse or fears for their safety, and the program page (IA-S13) lists survivors of sexual assault without mentioning a complaint; check this with the program before telling a survivor who has not reported that they qualify. Certification lasts four years (9E.3(3)). Iowa Code 9E.7 makes information the Secretary holds about applicants and participants confidential. Applications are mailed to Safe at Home, P.O. Box 959, Des Moines, IA 50304 (IA-S13, IA-S14); phone 515-725-7233. Record confidentiality: Iowa Code 915.90(1) says records confidential under 22.7 (which covers hospital, medical, and counselor records, IA-S12 22.7(2)) and information received from them remain confidential when the program obtains them. The application's release form (IA-S5) also says 'Iowa and federal law requires the CVC Program to keep confidential all confidential information received' and that mental health, drug or alcohol treatment, and HIV screening records are kept confidential. No Iowa statute or rule was found that makes the claim itself or the applicant's identity exempt from public records requests; 22.7 has no victim compensation entry.

jurisdictions.name: Idaho

program.agency: Idaho Industrial Commission, Crime Victims Compensation Program
program.statute_citation: Idaho Code 72-1001 to 72-1026; Idaho Code 19-5303; IDAPA 17.10.01

coverage.notes: No minimum loss amount appears in Idaho Code 72-1001 to 72-1026 or IDAPA 17.10.01. The statute and program pages do not list relocation, home security, temporary housing, or childcare as covered expenses, and I found no explicit exclusion either, so they are left out rather than marked excluded. Crime-scene cleanup is marked excluded from the FAQ restitution answer (ID-EXCL-5); the statute has no cleanup benefit and excludes property damage, but that FAQ sentence also wrongly lists wage loss as not covered. Replacement clothing or bedding is not listed anywhere; it would most likely fall under the property damage or loss exclusion, but no source says so directly. Wage loss has a one week waiting period under 72-1019(1) that is not modeled as a minimum loss. Transportation is reimbursed at the state employee mileage rate, which no saved source states as a number. IDAPA 17.10.01.013.07 also requires treatment and forensic exam bills to be submitted within three years of the date of treatment or eligibility; this is a bill deadline, not the claim filing deadline, so it is not encoded as a rule. Privacy: Idaho's Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Secretary of State under Idaho Code title 19, chapter 57 (ID-S16, ID-S17, ID-S15); sexual assault survivors are eligible, and an application based on sexual assault must include evidence such as police or court records, documentation from a sexual assault program, a professional's documentation, or a protection order (19-5703(2)). Compensation program records are confidential and exempt from public records disclosure under Idaho Code 72-1007 (ID-S14).

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statutes are from legislature.idaho.gov (the site notes it is updated each July 1). The exam_no_bill rule on private insurance (ID-EXAM-3) comes from the program page citing Idaho Code 19-5303 and 72-1019(2); the statute itself says the commission pays after federal or federally financed third parties for adults and after any liable third party for minors, which is consistent with the page. No statute found that flatly forbids billing the survivor for the exam; 72-1026(2) bars balance billing after the program pays, with an exception in 72-1026(3) when the program cannot pay the full allowable amount. The 72 hour police report rule has a good cause exception in statute; the program's exam-only reimbursement form (ID-S13) lets adults get the exam paid without reporting, but full benefits still require reporting or good cause. ID-CAP-1 cap language in 72-1019(5)(a) is drafted around death cases but the program pages state a $25,000 maximum for all claims. The FAQ restitution answer lists wage loss among things the program does not cover, which conflicts with 72-1019(1); the statute controls and that sentence was not used. Persons serving a sentence of imprisonment are ineligible under 72-1016(6). Reviewer: the exam-only (not reported) route on the program page also requires the crime to have occurred in Idaho and the application to be filed within one year or with good cause, and the page warns it may not cover all costs of the medical visit. Funeral cap ($5,000, 72-1019(4)) added for completeness. The FAQ restitution sentence that wrongly lists wage loss is now quoted only for its crime-scene cleanup exclusion (ID-EXCL-5), with the conflict stated in that rule's summary. How to file: the June 2026 application (ID-S11), the Complete an Application page (ID-S10), and the forensic exam page (ID-S8) all list the same three methods: email, fax, and mail.
