The program page agrees with the statute on the $25,000 total cap, the $300 per week wage cap, the 96-hour report, and the one-year filing deadline; the page states the wage cap as 'up to 16 weeks' and the rule as a $4,800 maximum (same total). Filing deadline runs from the date of the police report, not the crime. Work loss is limited to four months from the crime and is not paid while sick or annual leave is available. Travel requires at least 150 miles round trip and vehicle rental is capped at $30 per day. If the claimant has no insurance or other collateral source, the program pays 80 percent of billed charges for eligible medical, dental, or mental health services (94-03-03-06(3)); the 2025 mental health policy form describes provider reimbursement at 80 percent of patient responsibility. Forensic exam: under N.D.C.C. 12.1-34-07 the acute exam (within 120 hours unless good cause) may not be charged to the survivor directly or through a third-party payer, and the Attorney General reimburses providers; the statute does not condition this on a police report. The program page notes crowdfunding may be treated as a collateral source and restitution or civil recovery must be repaid. Contributory misconduct rule 94-03-03-05 lists conduct that requires denial; Tend shows conduct rules as information only. Reviewer: N.D.C.C. 12.1-34-07(2) separately bars charging a child forensic exam (criminal sexual conduct, physical abuse, or neglect) to the child or parent, and is recorded as ND-EXAM-CHILD. How to file: North Dakota has no PDF application. The program page says the application is online only (portalapps.nd.gov/docr/cvc-application/), so application_form is null with fillable false and field_count 0; the portal page could not be saved (blocked or empty, also through Chrome), so the application's own field list comes from the CVC Application Tips PDF (ND-S6). No official source states a mail, email, or fax filing method for the application itself; the program page and admin rule 94-03-01 give P.O. Box 1898, Bismarck, ND 58502-1898, fax 701-328-0309, and DOCRcompensation@nd.gov only as contact and correspondence details, and the employer and physician work-loss forms (ND-S10, ND-S11) are returned by mail, email, or fax. Supporting documents come from the 94-03-03 verification rules and the DOCR forms. Processing time (2 to 4 weeks) is from the program page. Privacy: N.D.C.C. 54-23.4-17 makes compensation records confidential, with inspection only by law enforcement for official duties or by a claimant's representative with the claimant's signed authorization; juvenile or law enforcement records obtained under chapter 27-20.4 are sealed at the end of proceedings. North Dakota has no address confidentiality program (Minnesota SOS directory lists 'North Dakota No Program'; no ND statute or agency page found), so no address_confidentiality rule was added. The Attorney General's Marsy's Law page describes a victim's right to prevent disclosure of information that could be used to locate the victim; that is not a substitute-address program.

jurisdictions.name: Nebraska

program.agency: Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice (Nebraska Crime Commission)
program.statute_citation: Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-1801 to 81-1842 (Nebraska Crime Victim's Reparations Act); 81-1429.03 (forensic exam payment); 80 Neb. Admin. Code chs. 1 to 5

coverage.notes: Lost wages are capped by regulation at the average weekly wage under the Nebraska Workers' Compensation Act (80 NAC ch. 3, 003.04), but no dollar figure is stated in the saved sources, so no lost_wages expense_cap rule was written. The regulation sets counseling, funeral, crime scene cleanup and direct medical provider limits by an Annual Rate Schedule set by the Committee, which I could not find online; the counseling cap of $5,000 comes from the program's current web page. No source mentions relocation, transportation, or home security as covered expenses. No dollar minimum loss was found; the only threshold is the more-than-seven-consecutive-days rule for wage loss on the application form.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute and agency sources disagree in places. (1) Police report window: 81-1821(1)(b) and the Oct 2023 application say five days; the FAQ PDF (updated 4-5-2023) still says three days. Statute wins. (2) Counseling cap: program web page and pamphlet say $5,000; the 2023 FAQ says $2,000; the regulation defers to an unpublished Annual Rate Schedule. Funeral: web page and pamphlet say $10,000, FAQ says $5,000. I used the current web page. (3) Out-of-state crimes: 81-1807(1) lets a Nebraska resident claim for a crime in a state with no program for which they are eligible, but 81-1824 says no order shall be made for offenses occurring outside the state. Left out of rules because of the conflict. (4) 81-1801(8) defines personal injury as actual bodily harm, while the program page describes victims as people physically or emotionally injured; worth a reviewer check for survivors without physical injury. (5) Forensic exam: 81-1429.03(5) lets the Sexual Assault Payment Program pay up to $200 for the examiner fee and $300 for the facility fee, with more payable on documentation; these are provider payment limits, not survivor caps, so they are not encoded. (6) 80 NAC ch. 3, 003.09 says a medical provider that accepts CVR payment accepts it as payment in full and is barred from collecting from the victim (saved in NE-S20). (7) The application requires a U.S. citizenship or qualified alien attestation under Neb. Rev. Stat. 4-108 to 4-114. (8) Regulations were saved from Cornell LII because rules.nebraska.gov is a JavaScript app and the old nebraska.gov PDF links redirect to it. Reviewer (Oct 3): added funeral ($10,000) and crime-scene cleanup ($5,000) caps from the current program page; the regulation (80 NAC ch. 3, 003.06 and 003.08, amended 11/10/2024) sets both by the unpublished Annual Rate Schedule, so these page figures may change. Split pain and suffering into its own excluded_expense rule and removed an example (a phone) that no source states. Added 81-1822(3) (no award if the victim's own criminal violation caused or contributed to the injury) as information only; the program says contributory conduct is never used to screen sexual assault claims (NE-S17). The wage rule NE-WAGE-1 is 'more than seven' consecutive days, so 7 days exactly does not qualify; it appears only on the Oct 2023 application form, not in the statute or regulation. 81-1823's $25,000 cap is 'Except as provided in section 81-1813', which was not saved. How to file (Oct 3): the Oct 2023 CVR Claim Application (NE-S15) is still the version linked from the program page; it is a flat PDF with no AcroForm fields (0 fields), so it must be printed or filled by hand. Submission is by mail or email per the program page and pamphlet; the fax number appears only in the application's return-to block next to the phone number, so NE-SUBMIT-3 is a reasonable reading rather than an explicit instruction. The program page lists the mailing address as Nebraska Crime Commission, 301 Centennial Mall South, P.O. Box 94946, Lincoln, NE 68509-4946; the application uses the shorter PO Box address, which I used. No online portal or in-person filing is stated. The 2023 FAQ (NE-S13) asks for 3 payroll stubs from just before the incident and an employer statement, while the Oct 2023 application asks for pay stubs for the missed periods and says CVR contacts the employer itself; I followed the application. Processing time: 81-1809(1), quoted in the saved Claims Process PDF (NE-S22; the statute itself was not saved), gives 180 days after all required information is received; the pamphlet says 6 to 9 months typically. Privacy (Oct 3): Nebraska's Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Secretary of State under the Address Confidentiality Act (Neb. Rev. Stat. 42-1201 and following). The program page (NE-S23) says it gives a substitute address for state and local agencies plus free first-class mail forwarding, and eligibility covers victims of abuse, sexual assault or stalking who fear for their safety and have recently moved or plan to move to a place unknown to the abuser. 42-1203(6) (NE-S24) defines sexual assault by reference to 28-319, 28-319.01, 28-320, 28-320.01 and 28-386, and the Act also covers trafficking victims (42-1203(8)). Enrollment is in person at a designated victim assistance center only; the program page says the Secretary of State's office does not accept applications. ACP contact per the page: (402) 471-3568 or toll free (866) 227-6327. Record confidentiality: 81-1842 (NE-S25) bars making public the name of a sexual assault victim in the committee's records when applying for compensation. It covers the name only; no saved source says the rest of the claim file is exempt from public records law. The Oct 2023 application (NE-S15) separately says its federal demographic data is used for statistical purposes only and kept confidential.

jurisdictions.name: New Hampshire

program.agency: New Hampshire Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General (Victims' Assistance Commission)
program.statute_citation: RSA 21-M:8-c; RSA 21-M:8-g to 21-M:8-k; N.H. Admin. Rules Jus 600

not_found: expense_cap for medical (no separate medical cap found; medical is limited only by the total cap and Medicaid fee-for-service rates)
expense_cap for lost_wages as a dollar amount (only 75% of wages for up to 3 months)
explicit rule on replacing personal property such as phones beyond the general property-loss exclusion
coverage.notes: The toll-free number 1-800-300-4500 works in New Hampshire only; out-of-state callers use (603) 271-1284 (both on NH-S1). The brochure PDF linked from the program page is an image-only file with no extractable text, so it was not saved. The total cap differs between sources: RSA 21-M:8-h, V says $50,000 per claimant per incident, while the program page says $40,000 per primary victim; the statute is used.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute vs program page: RSA 21-M:8-h, V (most recently amended 2022) sets a $50,000 maximum; the DOJ web page still says $40,000. The rule uses the statute. Reporting: Jus 605.02(c) requires a report within 5 days unless good cause is shown, and the application asks the same; the web FAQ only says to report unless there is a reasonable explanation. Jus 605.13(h) deems a sexual assault survivor who sought the exam or treatment to have reported to law enforcement. Exam billing: RSA 21-M:8-c covers any physical exam of a victim of an alleged sexual offense, while Jus 605.13 uses the words felonious sexual assault. Under Jus 605.13(c)(3), a survivor covered by Medicaid or Medicare whose kit is not anonymous is billed to Medicaid or Medicare by the provider; private insurance is billed only if the survivor chooses, and deductibles and co-pays are paid or reimbursed by the department. Hospital care: Jus 605.03(e)(2)-(3) bars hospital-care awards for an insured victim unless free or reduced-fee care has been denied. Relocation (Jus 605.07) requires a continuing credible threat and either a police report plus restraining order, or an advocate letter, and the move must happen within 6 months of the award. The program page and Jus 606.07 list different mailing addresses (1 Granite Place South vs 33 Capitol Street); the application form uses 33 Capitol Street. Jus 600 was readopted effective 12-9-19 (#12938). Reviewer additions: Jus 605.13(a) exam and treatment no-charge rule, 605.13(a) follow-up care, 605.13(c)(3) Medicaid/Medicare billing exception, 605.13(f) HIV prophylaxis voucher, 605.03(d)(4) replacement of assistive devices such as eyeglasses, and 605.03(e)(2) hospital-care limit for insured victims. Jus 605.13(e): if the exam is sought within 10 days the survivor agrees to evidence collection; an anonymous kit is kept 60 days for the survivor to decide whether to report, then destroyed. The $50,000 statutory cap was rechecked against the current gc.nh.gov text of RSA 21-M:8-h, V. How to file: the application (NH-S2, rev. 02/11/2021, the version linked from the program page today; Jus 604.01 still names an older 8/23/19 revision) is a flat PDF with no fillable fields, to be printed, signed, and mailed. The form's only stated filing method is mail to 33 Capitol Street; the program page's contact block lists 1 Granite Place South, so both are kept as mail rules and a survivor should confirm by phone. The program page lists a fax number and the victimcomp@doj.nh.gov email as contact details only; no source says applications may be filed by fax, email, online, or in person, so no rules were added for those methods. Police reports are not a survivor document: program staff request them from law enforcement (NH-S1, Jus 604.04(b)). Processing: first contact within 2 weeks (program page) and a decision no more than 60 days after a completed application reaches the agenda (Jus 603.03(f)); the program page also says it may take several months or longer. Privacy: the Address Confidentiality Program is created by RSA 7:41 to 7:51 and run by the Attorney General (RSA 7:41 purpose, NH-S7; RSA 7:43 application, sworn statement, and 4-year certification, NH-S8). The DOJ ACP page (NH-S9) says applicants must first go through one of the state's crisis centers, that participants use the substitute address for state and local services with first class mail (not packages) forwarded, and that a restraining order, charges, or a police report are not required; ACP phone (603) 271-8710, sexual assault line 1-800-277-5570. The ACP only works for a new address not yet on any state or local record. Record confidentiality comes from Jus 603.02(i); the sexual assault exam billing forms are separately kept confidential like medical records under RSA 21-M:8-c (NH-S6).

jurisdictions.name: New Jersey

program.agency: New Jersey Office of the Attorney General, Department of Law and Public Safety, Victims of Crime Compensation Office
program.statute_citation: N.J.S.A. 52:4B-1 et seq. (Criminal Injuries Compensation Act of 1971); N.J.A.C. 13:75

not_found: medical expense cap (none found beyond the $25,000 total)
reporting alternatives for sexual assault (none in statute or rules)
insurance billing rule for forensic exams
photo_id or proof of residency (the application and instructions do not ask for either)
coverage.notes: No source names which agency pays providers for the forensic exam, and none says whether a hospital may bill the survivor's insurance for it; the statute (52:4B-52(k), echoed in 52:4B-22(b)) bars charging the victim a fee for exam services, and the AG SART standards say care beyond the exam can be billed under hospital policy. Statute and regulation require a police or law enforcement report within nine months, with a good-cause exception for late reports; the AG SART standards also tell survivors that VCCO benefits require a report to law enforcement. No protective-order, advocate or exam-only alternative was found in law.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text: N.J.S.A. 52:4B-18 and 52:4B-52 from Justia's 2025 edition (the legislature site was not used); other sections from the OAG compilation dated 8/1/2020, which may predate later amendments (the 2024 VCCO FAQ mentions new covered crime types such as harassment and criminal mischief that are not in that compilation). The OAG administrative code copy has no visible adoption date but reflects post-August 2020 changes. The 2024 FAQ (NJ-S4) says a crime 'must have been reported to law enforcement within 9 months of the crime, filing of a restraining order or sexual violence protective order'; the statute (52:4B-18) says only police or law enforcement, so I did not record a protective-order alternative. The AG SART Standards (NJ-S13, 2018) say emergency care beyond the scope of the forensic exam may be charged under hospital policy, so the no-fee rule covers exam services only. The VCCO Eligibility page (NJ-S2) says the toll-free line 877-658-2221 is out of order and lists (973) 648-2107; the Contact page and OVC directory still list 877-658-2221. Counseling also has per-session rate caps by provider type in N.J.A.C. 13:75-4.4(a), not encoded. Catastrophic injury claims can get supplemental rehabilitative compensation beyond $25,000 (not encoded). Reviewer (Oct 3): moved NJ-CRIME-1 to Justia's 2025 text of 52:4B-11 (NJ-S18, amended through P.L.2023, c.101); the sexual assault offenses are unchanged and harassment and criminal mischief are not in that text, so the 2024 FAQ's mention of them is unconfirmed in statute. Changed the program phone to (973) 648-2107 because the Eligibility page (NJ-S2) says the toll-free line 877-658-2221 is out of order; the Contact page still lists both. Emergency award statute text (52:4B-10.1, NJ-S8) is from the 8/1/2020 compilation; its $7,500 per-award cap matches N.J.A.C. 13:75-5.1(c). The $3,000 security rule (NJ-SEC-1) is the same $3,000 as relocation, not an additional amount; an engine must not add them. N.J.A.C. 13:75-4.4(c) says a provider who accepts VCCO payment must accept the VCCO rate as payment in full and not seek more from other sources (not encoded; it is not exam-specific). Catastrophically injured victims can get up to $35,000 more for rehabilitative services under N.J.A.C. 13:75-6.3(a) (not encoded). How to file (Oct 3): the paper application (NJ-S16, rev. 8/25/20, effective 8/1/20) is still the version linked from the VCCO Paper Application page (NJ-S19); it has no AcroForm fields (field_count 0), so it is print-and-fill. Filing methods from the Contact page (NJ-S6): online at www.njvictims.org, fax 973-648-3937, or mail; the instructions give the mail address as VCCO, 50 Park Place, 5th floor, Newark, NJ 07102 (line breaks shown as commas in the target). The 2024 FAQ (NJ-S4) describes filing as completing the online application, so online is the main path. Email (njvictims@njvictims.org) is given only for status questions and appointment requests, not for filing, so no email submission rule; walk-ins are mentioned only in a closure notice, so no in_person rule. Claimants with an active claim and PIN can upload documents online; documents sent later should include the claim number (NJ-S6). The 90-day decision time in N.J.A.C. 13:75-4.2(c) (NJ-TIME-1) runs from acknowledgment of a complete application and can be extended for good cause; the instructions' 3 months (NJ-TIME-2) runs from receipt of all documentation. The Paper Application page also says to call if no receipt letter arrives within four weeks (not encoded). Most documents are 'if available'; the VCCO will request the police report itself if the survivor does not have one. Homicide-only documents (victim's tax returns for loss of support) were not encoded. Privacy (Oct 3): NJ-ACP-1 quotes the ACP purpose clause in N.J.S.A. 47:4-2 (Justia 2025, NJ-S22, amended 2019, c.175), which names victims of sexual assault; the DCF ACP page (NJ-S20) says the program gives a legal substitute address to survivors of domestic violence, stalking, sexual violence and reproductive health patients and providers, and that all state and local government agencies must accept it. The enroll text is copied from N.J.A.C. 3A:71-3.1(b) (Cornell LII, NJ-S21, amended effective 6/3/2024). Eligibility limits that matter for anonymity: the DCF page says applicants must have experienced fear or threat of abuse and must relocate, and ACP cannot remove addresses already publicly recorded; N.J.A.C. 3A:71-3.1(b)1iii requires a sworn statement that the abuse was reported to a law enforcement agency and/or court or that the applicant applied for an order under N.J.S.A. 2C:14-13 et seq. (a sexual assault protective order), so ACP is not available to a survivor who has made no report and sought no order. The DCF 'How to Apply' link is a video, not text, so it was not used. NJ-REC-1 is N.J.A.C. 13:75-1.6(b) from the OAG administrative code copy already saved (NJ-S9); the next sentence adds that victim and claimant files shall not be open to inspection by any person unless authorized by law or court order. I did not look for a separate statute on VCCO record confidentiality.

jurisdictions.name: New Mexico

program.agency: New Mexico Crime Victims Reparation Commission
program.statute_citation: NMSA 1978, Sections 31-22-1 to 31-22-24 (Crime Victims Reparation Act); 10.40.2 NMAC

not_found: expense_cap:lost_wages (no dollar or week cap found)
expense_cap:medical (no separate cap found; total cap applies)
coverage.notes: Relocation, security and temporary housing are not named in the statute, the rules, or the program FAQ. Section 31-22-9(C) allows 'any other pecuniary loss' the commission finds reasonable and proper, but I did not treat that as coverage for any specific item. No minimum loss amount was found. Address confidentiality: New Mexico's Safe at Home program (Confidential Substitute Address Act, NMSA 40-13B) is run by the Secretary of State; the SOS program and eligibility pages (NM-S15, NM-S16) name survivors of sexual assault and attempted sexual assault as eligible. Record confidentiality: 10.40.2.14 NMAC makes CVRC application files containing confidential medical and police records confidential with no public disclosure; no separate statute in 31-22 NMSA was found.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is from Justia's 2025 New Mexico Statutes (the CVRC site links NMOneSource, which did not load for scripts); 2026 session changes were not checked. 10.40.2 NMAC (State Records Center copy) was last amended 08/31/2006 and predates the 2019 amendment (Laws 2019, ch. 211) to 31-22-7 and 31-22-14. 10.40.2.9 NMAC still says sexual assault victims must report to law enforcement within 180 days; the 2019 statute removed the police-reporting deadline and allows a report to a licensed medical, mental health or counseling provider, or tribal health provider. Statute wins, so the 180-day rule is NOT encoded. The 2019 amendment also deleted the statutory good-cause extension for late applications, but the CVRC FAQ still says 'Some exceptions may be allowed for good cause'; the extension field reflects both. The 10/2025 brochure says an application must be filed 'within a reasonable time' (its PDF text extraction is garbled, so it is not quoted). The CVRC FAQ says the cap is $50,000 in cases of permanent physical disability; the statute says $20,000 plus up to $30,000 more for catastrophic injury resulting in permanent total disability. Forensic exam payment: NMSA 29-11-7 assigns free exams to the 'administrator', which 29-11-3 defines as the director of the mental health division of the Department of Health or a designee. I could not verify from an official source which office administers exam payment today. The transportation rate (twenty cents per mile) is in the summary and quote only, because the params schema stores money as dollars. Reviewer: the CVRC FAQ and the 10/2025 brochure both say 'The crime must have occurred in New Mexico', but 31-22-3(I)(2)-(3) also covers New Mexico residents injured in a state with no eligible compensation program and residents injured by international terrorism; the statute is encoded. 10.40.2.10(L) NMAC still says the victim must cooperate with law enforcement in the prosecution; the 2019 statute lets the commission accept that the victim acted reasonably instead, so the statute is encoded. The 'mental health division of the department of health' named in 29-11-3 was last renamed in 1995; whether that office still exists or pays exams today was not confirmed. How to file: the CVRC application page links the online portal at https://cvcapp.cvrc.nm.gov (the link target, saved as NM-S14). No official source says to email the application, so no email rule was added even though the form header and contact pages list cvrc@cvrc.nm.gov (and the contact page and brochure list cvrc.office@cvrc.nm.gov). 10.40.2.8(B) NMAC says a paper application counts when 'postmarked delivered or faxed' to the commission's offices; 'delivered' is not clearly in-person filing, so no in_person rule was added. The current English application (Reviewed 02/2025, NM-S3) is the one linked from the Documents to Download page; it is fillable with 135 AcroForm fields. Document requirements for receipts, lost wages and counseling come from 10.40.2.10 NMAC (2006); the application itself asks only for a police report if available, a death certificate or power of attorney where relevant, and the signed authorization. The 10/2025 brochure says bills or records can be uploaded in the online application, but its PDF text is garbled, so it is not quoted. Safe at Home: NMSA 40-13B-3 (NM-S17, Justia 2025) describes the program as protecting 'a victim of domestic violence'; the statutory definition section (40-13B-2) was not saved, so covers_sexual_assault rests on the Secretary of State pages, which list survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, attempted sexual assault and stalking. The SOS eligibility page also says applicants must have recently relocated or plan to move, certification lasts three years, and program records are confidential and not subject to the Inspection of Public Records Act. The enroll text is copied from the SOS eligibility page (NM-S16), not from the rule's quoted source. Record confidentiality comes from the 2006 administrative rule (10.40.2.14 NMAC); it covers application files that contain confidential medical and police records, and I did not find a statute in the Crime Victims Reparation Act declaring all claim records confidential.

jurisdictions.name: Nevada

program.agency: Nevada Department of Human Services, Division of Child and Family Services
program.statute_citation: NRS 217.010 to 217.270; sexual assault exams and county treatment: NRS 217.280 to 217.350

not_found: minimum_loss (no minimum out-of-pocket loss found in NRS 217 or the State Plan)
emergency_award (none; the program says it is not an emergency funded program and the application says it does not provide emergency or immediate financial assistance)
exam_no_bill.insurance_billing (NRS 217.300 bars charging the survivor directly but says nothing on billing the survivor's insurance)
expense_cap:transportation (mileage is not paid; receipted travel is discretionary with only a $50 meal per diem)
reporting_requirement.within_days (the current statute sets no police-reporting deadline for compensation)
coverage.notes: Statute wins over older agency text. Filing deadline: NRS 217.100 (Rev. 4/15/2026, amended 2025) gives 60 months, or 60 months after age 21 for minors; the eligibility page (NV-S1) still says two years and the 2020 State Plan (NV-S7 300.2) says 24 months, so those are not used. Police reports: NRS 217.100(5) lets eligibility be shown by other documents and the 2026 instructions (NV-S9) say reports are not required, but the eligibility page (NV-S1, 5-day report rule), the application page (NV-S3), the 7/30/2026 application form (NV-S4), and the 2020 State Plan 200.1 and 300.12(A) still describe a police report requirement; that conflict is recorded here and the statute is followed. The rule caps for wages, relocation, lodging, security, childcare, and prescriptions come from the July 1, 2020 State Plan, which the program's Regulations page links as current; it says benefit levels may change at any time. Counseling ($5,000), medical and dental ($35,000), and cleanup ($5,000) come from the current coverage-limits page. NV-S9 says counseling and crime-scene cleanup may be covered beyond the $35,000 total. Reviewer additions: the 7/30/2026 application form (NV-S4) asks for a reason only when the crime occurred more than five years ago, which matches the 60-month statute. NRS 217.210, which the 7/30/2026 form still cites for police reports, does not appear in the Rev. 4/15/2026 chapter text. The 2026 instructions (NV-S9) list the crime being reported to law enforcement or another appropriate authority as an eligibility condition while also saying law enforcement reports are not required, so a survivor may still be asked for some official record. The coverage-limits page also caps chiropractic and physical therapy at $5,000 and medical equipment and supplies at $2,500; those fit no single expense type and are not encoded. Confidential Address Program: the DCFS program page (NV-S10) says the program covers victims of sexual assault, and the statute (NRS 217.462 in NV-S5) also lists sexual assault and lets the Division approve an application backed by specific evidence such as a record of conviction or a protective order. Record confidentiality comes from NRS 217.105.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Main source conflicts: (1) filing deadline 60 months in NRS 217.100 vs two years/24 months on the eligibility page and in the 2020 State Plan; (2) police report required on older agency pages and the 7/30/2026 application form vs not required under NRS 217.100(5) and the 2026 application instructions. Other things a reviewer should know but that fit no category: NRS 217.220(4) lets the officer deny an award if the applicant will not suffer serious financial hardship, without counting the home, one vehicle, or savings up to one year's salary; NRS 217.245 says a provider that accepts VOCP payment takes it as payment in full and may not bill the victim further. NRS 217.310 to 217.340 separately let a sexual assault survivor (and spouse) apply to the county for medical and counseling treatment up to $1,000, with its own 60-day application or 3-day report timing; that county benefit is not encoded as a VOCP rule. The 2020 State Plan 400.15 limit of $1,000 for a sexual assault exam in rural counties predates the 2025 amendment of NRS 217.300 that pays exams from the Fund, so it is not encoded. Counseling hourly rates on the coverage-limits page ($125 psychiatrist down to $45 intern) are provider rates and are not encoded. The OVC directory (ovc.ojp.gov/states/nevada) lists the program at voc.nv.gov, phone 702-486-2740; it was read but not saved as a source. The NAC Chapter 217 was checked and only covers fictitious addresses, so it was not saved. Reviewer: NV-S7 kind changed from regulation to agency_pdf because the State Plan is program policy under NRS 217.094, not an administrative code. filing_deadline uses months (60) and from: age_21 because the statute counts in months and from age 21; the schema lists only years/days and age_18, so the engine must handle these values. How to file: the application page (NV-S3) links the 7/30/2026 form (NV-S4), so NV-S4 is program.application_form (fillable AcroForm, 176 fields). NV-S9, the 2026 instructions-plus-form PDF in the voc-forms-2026 folder, is also fillable (182 fields) and gives the same mail address, email, and fax; it is used here only for the release-form and crime-documentation requirements. Submission: mail to 500 E. Warm Springs Rd, Suite 100, Las Vegas, NV 89119; email vocp-applications@dcfs.nv.gov; fax (702) 486-2825. NV-S9's cover page lists vocp@dcfs.nv.gov as a general email, but the signature page says to send applications to vocp-applications@dcfs.nv.gov, so only that one is encoded. No online filing portal was found. The office address on NV-S3 is where applicants can get help in person; no source says applications may be dropped off there, so in_person is not encoded. Documents: NV-S9 says to submit whatever documents you have now and send more later, and says eligible applicants will be sent a checklist of specific documents for each benefit; the lost wage section says a social security number must be included. Processing time comes from NRS 217.110(2) (60 days after receipt of the application, with a 5-day denial window when ineligibility is apparent); the 2020 State Plan 600.1 says the same 60 days. Confidential Address Program: NRS 217.462 to 217.471 (in NV-S5) set up the fictitious address program run by the Division of Child and Family Services (the Division is defined in NRS 217.400); administration moved there from the Attorney General in 2017, and the Attorney General's old CAP pages still show up in search, so the DCFS page (NV-S10) is used. NV-S10 says approved participants are enrolled for four years and lists the program's phone and email for finding a Certified Advocate; these are not encoded as params. NV-S10's eligibility list says applicants need specific evidence of victimization, and NRS 217.462(4) gives a conviction record or a protective order as examples, which may be a barrier for survivors who never reported. Record confidentiality: NRS 217.105 makes claim information confidential with three exceptions (applicant or attorney request, necessary administration of the chapter, court order); NRS 217.110 separately covers availability and confidentiality of law enforcement reports used in a claim and is not encoded.

jurisdictions.name: New York

program.agency: New York State Office of Victim Services (OVS)
program.statute_citation: N.Y. Executive Law Article 22 (sections 620 to 635); 9 NYCRR Part 525; Public Health Law 2805-i

coverage.notes: total_cap: Article 22 sets no overall maximum award; it caps specific categories (lost earnings, relocation, property, etc.) and medical and counseling costs have no dollar cap in the statute. I did not record a total cap rather than infer one. Counseling rates: no per-session counseling fee cap was found in Executive Law 631 or in 9 NYCRR 525.3 or 525.12; 525.12(g)(4) lets OVS require proof that counseling is crime-related when a claim is filed more than one year after counseling began. minimum_loss: no minimum out-of-pocket loss requirement was found in the statute sections read. Security: covered for new or enhanced devices with a physician, counselor, or DA statement (525.12(g)(3)); no dollar cap found apart from the $2,500 crime scene securing cap. Financial difficulty: Exec. Law 631(6)(a) requires a finding of financial difficulty except for emergency awards and awards under ten thousand dollars (not a schema category). Reporting: the old one-week police reporting rule is no longer in Exec. Law 631(1); the current text accepts records of a support agency for survivors of crime. OVS pages say the Crime Verification Form is accepted only for claims filed on or after December 31, 2025. Reviewer additions: 9 NYCRR 525.12(h)(9) (LII text, last amended 2022) says direct-reimbursement exam expenses must relate to services within 120 hours of the incident, waived for a child victim or for good cause, and no kit reimbursement past 120 hours; the current Exec. Law 631(13) and the March 2026 OVS provider billing manual do not state this window, so it is not encoded as a rule. The per-item clothing, bedding, communication and transportation-item limits in 525.12(n)(1)-(4) do not apply when OVS finds the property is related to the victim's health or safety (525.12(n)(6)); the $2,500 statutory property cap still applies. The protective-order, victim services provider, and medical or mental health provider alternatives in Exec. Law 631(1)(c)(iii) are conditioned in the statute on the victim being unable to report to or cooperate with police for health or safety reasons; the OVS update page (NY-S7) describes the Crime Verification Form without that condition. processing_time: no saved OVS page, application, or statute section states a time for a decision or payment, so none is recorded.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is from the NY Senate Open Legislation site (fetched via Chrome). 9 NYCRR text is from Cornell LII because the official Westlaw NYCRR site is script-heavy; LII shows the 525.12 amendment history through Oct 12, 2022, and its funeral cap ($6,000) is older than the current statute ($12,000 in Exec. Law 631(2)), so for any conflict the statute wins. Effective dates from OVS update pages: three-year filing deadline and Crime Verification Form alternative to police reports apply starting December 31, 2025; filing deadline previously shorter. Exec. Law 631(13)(b) also sets provider reimbursement ceilings for the exam ($800 / $1,200 / $2,500); these are provider rates, not survivor-facing, so I did not encode them. The OVS FRE page says claims received on or after February 3, 2026 are paid by a new OVS fee schedule. PHL 2805-i(1) has two versions of the no-billing paragraph (lettered (d) until May 9, 2027 and (g) after); the quoted text is identical in both. Expense caps with per='item' (clothing, communication items) are per-item limits from 9 NYCRR 525.12(n); per='item' is outside the schema's listed values but is what the regulation says. A phone would most plausibly fall under 'ability to communicate', but the regulation does not name phones. Essential personal property awards for adults generally require a physical injury; sex offense victims are presumed physically injured under Exec. Law 626(1). The older OVS FAQ page and 2022 guideline PDFs state superseded rules (one-week reporting, one-year filing, $500 property cap), so I did not use them. How to file: the English application link on the OVS page (ovs.ny.gov/compensation_application_english) still redirects to the Feb. 2026 fillable PDF saved as NY-S4 (552 AcroForm fields), so that is the newest version. Submission targets come from the application's contact section: mail to the Albany AE Smith Building address and email to OVSIntake@ovs.ny.gov; online filing is through OVS Compass (program.apply_url). The OVS page (NY-S1) also lists a Brooklyn office at 55 Hanson Place for the Compensation Division, but the application says to mail documents to the Albany address, so only Albany is encoded. No fax or in-person filing method is stated. The application also says documents can be sent later if not ready, and the OVS page says OVS may later ask for birth or death certificates, marriage licenses, insurance Explanations of Benefits, and receipts depending on the claim; those on-request items are not encoded as required documents. Photo ID, proof of residency, and wage verification are not requested up front; for lost wages the application says OVS contacts the employer. Address confidentiality: Exec. Law 108 (NY-S21) makes victims of a sexual offense (Penal Law article 130 and 255.25 to 255.27, including threats or attempts) eligible for the Department of State Address Confidentiality Program; applicants affirm they left their residence because of the acts and fear for their safety (108(2)(a)(i)), applications are filed with the office of the secretary (108(2)(c)), designated state, local or nonprofit agencies assist applicants (108(3)), and certification lasts four years (108(2)(e)). The DOS ACP pages (NY-S22, NY-S23) still describe eligibility as victims of domestic violence only and say participation is limited to New York State residents; the statute is broader and wins, so covers_sexual_assault is true from the statute. The enroll text and contact details come from the DOS apply page (NY-S23). Record confidentiality: Exec. Law 633(1) (NY-S20) exceptions are legitimate criminal justice requests (where the victim reported to a victim services provider instead of police, OVS may not share identifying information), judicial subpoenas, requests by the victim or claimant or their authorized representative, and purposes necessary for administering Article 22; 633(2) makes other OVS records (such as those under 631-a and 632-a) public; 633(3) keeps records that are confidential under other laws confidential.

jurisdictions.name: Ohio

program.program_name: Ohio Victims of Crime Compensation Program
program.agency: Ohio Attorney General, Crime Victim Services Section

not_found: expense_cap for counseling for the victim
coverage.notes: No statute, rule, or official page I could save sets a weekly wage cap, a per-session counseling cap for the victim, or any relocation, housing, or transportation benefit. The application lists 'Mileage' as a checkbox but I found no rule text describing it. Security repairs are covered only as part of crime scene cleanup (ORC 2743.51(T)(2), $750 per claim). The statute requires that the crime was reported to law enforcement at some point and lists no alternative (forensic exam, advocate, protective order) for sexual assault. The Attorney General's HTML program pages (Apply for Victims Compensation, SAFE Program) could not be saved by the fetch tool, so the application PDF and brochure stand in for them. Privacy (added Oct 3): Safe at Home is Ohio's address confidentiality program (ORC 111.41 to 111.47, Secretary of State). For compensation records I found only ORC 2743.62(A)(2)(a), which keeps already-confidential records (for example medical records) confidential in the AG's or Court of Claims' hands; I found no statute or official statement making the whole claim, application, or applicant identity confidential or exempt from public records law.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statutes are from codes.ohio.gov (ORC 2743.51, 2743.56, 2743.60 effective March 2, 2022 after S.B. 36). Disagreements: the AG brochure 'Crime Can Be Costly' (OH-S15, undated) says family counseling is capped at $2,500 per person or $7,500 per family, but ORC 2743.60(H) caps an (L)(2) immediate-family claimant at $5,000; I used the statute. The Court of Claims FAQ (OH-S12) still says certain serious criminal history disqualifies, but the AG's own Apply for Victims Compensation page (read during research but not savable with the fetch tool) says that as of March 2, 2022 criminal backgrounds are no longer disqualifiers, matching the amended ORC 2743.60. Exam billing: per the AG SAFE instructions (OH-S14), emergency contraception, pain medication, and treatment of injuries beyond the forensic exam may be billed to the patient or insurer; those costs can then be claimed as medical expenses. Ohio health care providers must report a sexual assault to police under ORC 2921.22 (an adult may stay unnamed), per OH-S14; I did not find authority saying that provider report satisfies the compensation reporting rule, so Tend should not assume it does. ORC 2743.521(B) (OH-S11) bars a medical provider that accepts payment through an award from billing the victim for those expenses. The application PDF lists phone 614-466-5610 and toll-free 877-584-2846 (877-5VICTIM); the OVC directory lists 614-466-5610. Reviewer: added OH-EXAM-5 to 7 and OH-CAP-6 from sources already saved. The free exam is limited to evidence collection: for adults the SAFE table makes procedures billable to the patient when the last incident was more than 96 hours earlier (absent documented extenuating circumstances), and with other injuries the ED level charge, physician charges, labs, scans, and HIV prophylaxis are listed as billable to the patient. OAC 109:7-1-02(C) lets the Attorney General raise the $632 and $2,500 amounts for inflation; the SAFE instructions still state $632, so I kept it, but the current figure could be higher. ORC 2743.60(F) and (I) also bar awards for crimes against adults while serving a prison sentence and suspend payment while a victim is incarcerated; there is no schema category for these. How to file (added Oct 3): the AG Apply for Victims Compensation page (OH-S16) lists online filing, mail, fax, and email. The fetch tool rejected that page as blocked because the site is ASP.NET and wraps all content in one <form>, which the tool strips; I saved the same Chrome snapshot with the tool's text extraction minus the form removal, so OH-S16.txt is that page's text. The online target is the 'Register and file' link in the saved HTML. ORC 2743.56(A) (OH-S4) says a mailed application counts as filed on its postmark date. The application PDF (OH-S9, same URL the Apply page links, modified June 2026) has 207 AcroForm fields. It asks for copies of 6 paychecks for lost wages, front and back of insurance cards, a death certificate for funeral claims, and a signed release; it does not tell applicants to attach bills, receipts, or a police report, so I did not add those. ORC 2743.59(E) (OH-S17) sets the 120-day decision limit, which the AG can extend in writing; no AG page states a typical processing time. A separate supplemental application exists for later expenses and was not saved. Privacy (added Oct 3): ORC 111.42(A)(3) (OH-S18) makes victims of rape or sexual battery eligible for Safe at Home; the Secretary of State page (OH-S20) also lists sexual assault and says participants must apply through a certified Application Assistant and get a substitute address for voter registration, government correspondence, and other official records. Certification lasts four years (ORC 111.42(E)); registered sex offenders are ineligible. Record confidentiality is narrow: ORC 2743.62(A)(2)(a) (OH-S19) only preserves the confidential status a record already had, and 2743.62(A)(2)(b) lets judges, magistrates, the claimant, and the AG refer to those records in hearings and written decisions. The Court of Claims page (OH-S12) says it keeps an electronic archive of Victims decisions back to 1977, so Tend should not tell Ohio users their claim is fully private. I did not find any ORC 149.43(A)(1) exemption naming compensation claim files.

jurisdictions.name: Oklahoma

program.agency: Oklahoma District Attorneys Council, Victim Services Division, Crime Victims Compensation Board

coverage.notes: No dollar minimum loss was found; program pages only say there must be economic loss. Relocation, security, and temporary housing are not listed as allowable expenses in 21 O.S. 142.3 or on the program pages, and no cap for the victim's own lost wages was found beyond the overall cap. Medical services are limited to 80% of cost rather than a dollar cap. No statute was found that expressly bars a provider from billing the survivor for exam charges above the $800 fund limit. Address confidentiality comes from the Attorney General's ACP page (statutory basis 22 O.S. 60.14, not saved here); record confidentiality comes from 21 O.S. 142.9(G).

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statutes (OSCN, 21 O.S. as amended by SB 420, eff. Nov 1, 2023) win over program pages. Conflicts: the DAC page and the 2019 claim form say the total cap is $20,000 ($40,000 with the wage add-on) and the filing deadline is one year; current 142.13(B) says $25,000 ($50,000) and 142.10(A)(1) says thirty months. The OCVC eligibility page says caregiver work loss is $2,000 but 142.13(A) and (K) say $3,000. 142.10(A)(1) still has a leftover phrase about extending 'beyond one (1) year' next to the new 30-month period. The Board may grant up to $25,000 beyond the base cap for wages or loss of support, with a hard ceiling of $50,000 under 142.13(B). The application PDF is the 2019 form and predates the 2023 changes; the online claim at ocvcapp.okvictimscomp.com is the primary route. OAC 185:10-1-4 still says one year and was not used. The filing_deadline rule uses a 'months' param because the schema only lists years or days. Exam: OAC 185:15-1-6(d) treats Medicaid or other federal programs as a collateral source that must deny first; private insurance is optional for the survivor and any insurance payment goes back to the fund (185:15-1-6(c)). Providers must stop debt collection once notified of a pending claim (21 O.S. 142.9(H)). Reviewer: the OCVC home page still says a claim should be filed within one year, and the eligibility page says 'within one (30) months'; the statute's 30 months controls. 142.3 on OSCN lists amendments only through 2007 even though its text mentions vehicle impound fees, so its history note may be incomplete. Vehicle impound fees are capped at $750 (142.13(L)) and homicide family crisis counseling at $3,000 (142.13(G)); neither was added as a rule because neither applies to a living sexual assault survivor. The DAC exam page says the $800 limit applies to assaults on or after November 1, 2023, so older assaults may fall under an earlier, lower limit that was not researched. How to file: the online portal (ocvcapp.okvictimscomp.com) is the main route; its page says written applications go by mail or fax, while the 2019 claim form says to print, sign, and then fax, email, or mail it, so email comes only from the form. The current printable application is still the June 2019 claim form (OK-S12), which the portal links; it is a flat PDF with no fillable fields (pypdf found 0), and the DAC page still links older 2016/2017 forms that were not used. No in-person filing method is stated. The police report is requested by the DA's Victim-Witness Coordinator, not attached by the survivor. Processing times come from program pages, not statute: the FAQ says 4 to 12 months overall, the DAC page says claims are docketed within 30 days of full documentation and paid within three weeks of approval. Privacy: the Oklahoma Attorney General runs the Address Confidentiality Program (OK-S26); its page lists sexual assault among covered crimes and says applicants must have recently relocated or be planning to move, and apply in person through a designated victim assistance program with an application assistant (no direct applications). Certification lasts four years per the page. The program's statutory basis is 22 O.S. 60.14, which was not saved. Claim records are confidential under 21 O.S. 142.9(G) (OK-S6), with discovery exceptions only for an APA appeal of a Board decision or a strict showing to a court. OAC 185:15-1-6(b) (OK-S20) also lets exam-fund survivors skip employment and insurance information to keep anonymity.

jurisdictions.name: Oregon

program.agency: Oregon Department of Justice, Crime Victim and Survivor Services Division
program.statute_citation: ORS 147.005 to 147.367 (compensation); ORS 147.395 to 147.399 (SAVE Fund); OAR 137-076 and 137-084

coverage.notes: No minimum out-of-pocket loss appears in ORS 147.005 to 147.367 or OAR 137-076, so minimum_loss is left out rather than assumed to be zero. No security (locks, alarms) or temporary housing benefit was found. Relocation is listed as excluded on the program page, so there is no relocation cap. Oregon has no statute that makes compensation records confidential by default: ORS 147.115(1) makes applicant information public unless the department decides to keep it confidential, so record_confidentiality is recorded as conditional.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute and rule text come from oregonlegislature.gov (ORS ch. 147, current edition with 2025 notes) and the Secretary of State OARD site (OAR 137-076 and 137-084, saved through the browser). Conflicts: (1) ORS 147.055 allows an emergency award up to $1,000, but the program page says CVC is unable to provide immediate financial assistance; the rule is kept because the statute governs, but in practice the program may not offer one. (2) OAR 137-084-0010(4) requires a complete SAFE Kit assessment within 84 hours of the assault for SAVE Fund payment, while the DOJ provider page lists 120 hours; the victim SAVE page says within seven days (matches the 168-hour partial assessment). (3) Statute sets transportation coverage when care is more than 30 miles away; agency pages say 60 miles roundtrip (consistent). OAR 137-076-0019(1)(e) states the rate as '.50 cents per mile'; the brochure says 50 cents per mile. (4) The FAQ says loss of support rose to $800/week; that applies to dependents of deceased victims only. Claims expire three years after the determination order (or at age 21 for minors), ORS 147.035(8). Toll-free number 1-800-503-7983 appears in the brochure. Under the SAVE FAQ, a survivor may choose to bill insurance instead of the SAVE Fund, in which case leftover copays go to a CVC application rather than the Fund. The limited counseling award ($5,000) is the path for survivors who never report and never get an exam or order. Strangulation (SKIT) exams are paid under ORS 147.035(2)(e) with a $5,000 maximum and are billed to insurance first, so they are not modeled as exam_no_bill. Reviewer: the SAVE Fund's $475 maximum (OAR 137-084-0020(1)(a)) is what the Fund pays the provider for an exam plus SAFE Kit collection, not a limit on what the survivor gets, and the provider cannot bill the survivor or insurance for the rest; it is therefore not modeled as an expense_cap. The limited counseling award (OR-CAP-COUNS-LTD, $5,000) and the parent lost wages cap (OR-CAP-WAGE-PARENT, $5,000) are conditional caps for applicants who do not meet eligibility and for parents of minor victims, not general caps on the victim's counseling or lost wages. How to file (added Oct 3): submission methods, documents, and timing come mainly from the 2026 fillable English application (OR-S7, 140 AcroForm fields), which is the newest version linked from the apply page. The apply page FAQ (OR-S5) gives the mailing address as '1162 Court St SE', but the 2026 application, the brochure, and the program page all say 1162 Court Street NE, so the mail rule uses NE. Page 2 of the application still lists the old email domain cvssd@doj.state.or.us; the instructions page uses cvssd@doj.oregon.gov, which is used here. The program page and brochure list fax 503-378-5738 as contact information but no source says to fax the application, so no fax submission rule was added. Decision timing differs by source: the 2026 application says 60 to 90 days, the FAQ says applicants are usually notified within 70 days, and the 2024 brochure says 45 to 60 days; the newest (application) is used. The application does not ask the survivor to attach a police report or medical records: it asks for the report number and provider details, and CVC requests medical records and police reports itself. Bills are submitted after the claim is accepted. Privacy (added Oct 3): Oregon's Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Oregon DOJ (not the Secretary of State) under ORS 192.820 to 192.868; ORS 192.822(1)(a) and 192.826(3) name victims of a sexual offense as eligible, and the DOJ page names survivors of sexual assault. Enrollment is only through a certified Application Assistant (a victim advocate designated by the Attorney General); the ACP FAQ says applicants must live in Oregon, be 18 or older (parents or guardians may apply for minors), and currently live at an address unknown to the perpetrator, so a recent confidential relocation is required, and participation lasts four years. ACP contact: P.O. Box 1108, Salem, OR 97308; 503-373-1323; toll-free in Oregon 1-888-559-9090; ACP@doj.oregon.gov. Record confidentiality is weak in Oregon: ORS 147.115(1) says applicant information is open to the public unless the department determines it should be confidential, with sexual offenses (rape, sodomy, sexual abuse) as one listed ground, and ORS 147.115(3) says board hearing records are public records. The 2026 application itself warns that 'this application may be subject to disclosure under public record law' (OR-S7, page 2), so Tend should tell Oregon survivors to ask CVC to keep their claim confidential under the sexual offense ground and avoid putting extra detail in the free-text field. Separately, ORS 147.397(5)(a) requires SAVE Fund exam providers to keep confidential the identity of victims who have not reported to police.

jurisdictions.name: Pennsylvania

program.agency: Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency (PCCD), Office of Victims' Services
program.statute_citation: Crime Victims Act, 18 P.S. 11.101 et seq. (compensation: 18 P.S. 11.701 to 11.710); 37 Pa. Code Chapter 411

not_found: excluded_expense:phones (no explicit statement; only general property exclusion)
coverage.notes: No source found that covers home security costs (locks, alarms, cameras); treat security as not covered unless the program confirms. Phones are not named anywhere; the general property loss/damage exclusion applies. The statute's emergency award limit is 'a rate set by the Office of Victims' Services'; the $5,000 figure comes from 37 Pa. Code 411.17 and matches the 2025 manual. Relocation lodging is $75 per day (PA-RELOC-4); relocation vehicle rental is $30 per day (37 Pa. Code 411.42(f)), not encoded separately. Travel caps (car rental $30/day, meals $28/day for trips of 50+ miles) are taken from the 2025 manual because the matching list in 37 Pa. Code 411.42(g) is introduced by a clause about death and funeral travel and reads ambiguously. Filing: the claim form (July 2024, the version linked from the PA.gov apply page) lists the mailing address, email, and the DAVE online portal; the PA.gov page also lists the Crime Victims App for online filing. The form's fax number (717-787-4306) is listed only as contact info and the manual mentions fax only for advocates sending supplemental bills, so no fax submission rule was added. No in-person filing method is stated.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Act 77 of 2022 changes (5-year filing deadline, 'promptly' reporting instead of 72 hours, $50 minimum loss, 701.1 counseling claims, conduct not considered for counseling) apply to crimes on or after 9/8/2022; for older crimes the program says to contact it (2-year deadline and 72-hour reporting applied before). 37 Pa. Code Chapter 411 was last amended in 2009 and still references some pre-2022 limits (for example a 1-year FRE provider deadline that is consistent with the 2024 FRE protocol); where regulations and statute differ the statute controls. The PA.gov page says 'The crime must have occurred in Pennsylvania', while the statute's definitions (18 P.S. 11.103) also cover Pennsylvania residents harmed outside the state when the other location's program is ineligible under VOCA; the manual narrows this to foreign countries without a program and international terrorism. Insurance: providers must bill the survivor's insurance first for the exam unless the survivor (or person responsible) asks that insurance not be billed (18 P.S. 11.707(h)(1); FRE protocol B.2), so insurance_billing is recorded as 'allowed' with a survivor opt-out. The PA.gov transportation flyer says 'A maximum payment of $35,000 per direct victim can be reimbursed for transportation expenses'; that is just the overall cap and is not encoded. The English VCAP brochure PDF is image-only and was not saved. Counseling for a minor whose insurance is held by the alleged perpetrator or a non-supportive caretaker may be paid without billing that insurance (18 P.S. 11.707(b)(4.1)(i)). Reviewer: the PA.gov page says the claim must be filed 'within 5 years of the crime'; the statute (18 P.S. 11.702(b)(1)) runs it from discovery, which the rule follows. The 37 Pa. Code 411.42(d) health-item limit says 'each' device and 'will not exceed $1,000'; encoded per claim, but it may be read per item. FRE FAQ: if the survivor declines evidence collection the hospital may bill the survivor's insurance (Q14), and medications without an exam are not paid on the FRE claim (Q11); both can go on a standard claim. Application form: PA-S6 (VCAP long claim form, July 2024) is a flat PDF with no AcroForm fields (0 fields), so it is not fillable; a short claim form and a separate FRE claim form also exist but were not saved. The 2025 manual cover gives the PO Box ZIP as 17110-1167, while the claim form and the manual's own sample letters use 17108-1167; the submission rule follows the claim form. The applicant does not need to attach a police report: the claim process flyer says VCAP obtains the police report itself and sends verification forms to providers and employers; the form asks for the police department and incident number. The 12-week figure is from the PA.gov FAQ ('Most organizations process claims in 12 weeks or less'), not the statute. Payments to providers are released 2 to 4 weeks after approval (PA-S13). Address confidentiality: the OVA ACP page (PA-S14) lists sexual assault victims as eligible and says enrollment is online, through a local victim service program, or by calling OVA; the statute (23 Pa.C.S. 6703(a)) says eligible persons 'shall receive a confidential substitute address provided by the Office of Victim Advocate'. The statute's definition of 'victim of sexual assault' (23 Pa.C.S. 6702) lists specific offenses (18 Pa.C.S. 3121 rape, 3133, 4302, 6312, 6318, 6320) and 6704(2) requires an affidavit that the applicant fears future violent acts by the perpetrator, so eligibility under the statute is narrower than the agency page wording; OVA decides. ACP records, including applications and actual addresses, are confidential and exempt from the Right-to-Know Law (23 Pa.C.S. 6703(d)). Participants renew every 3 years per the OVA page. Record confidentiality: 18 P.S. 11.709(b) bars disclosure without the written consent of the direct victim or intervenor, except as otherwise provided by law; 11.709(c) still allows use in OVS appeal hearings, in enforcing section 1303, and in talking with the prosecutor about restitution. The Act 77 flyer (PA-S7) restates this.

jurisdictions.name: Rhode Island

program.agency: Rhode Island Office of the General Treasurer

coverage.notes: No Rhode Island statute or official policy was found that bars billing the survivor or the survivor's insurance for a sexual assault forensic exam; the only official statement found is the Attorney General's bill of rights saying the exam cost is compensable through the CVCP regardless of reporting. No minimum loss was found. The relocation cap is in flux: the compiled statute (12-25-21.1(e)) and the current rule say $5,000, but a 2026 bill (H 8155) raised it to $8,000 and the amended rule effective 10/13/2026 (RI-S14) says $8,000, so no relocation dollar cap is recorded. Counseling hourly rates, the $1,000 travel cap, the 62% lost-earnings rule, the property exclusion, and the reporting rules appear in both the current rule (RI-S11) and the amended rule effective 10/13/2026 (RI-S14). No processing time for a decision or payment is stated in the program page, the application, or the rule; the only stated times are 30 days for a decision on reconsideration, which is not recorded. The address confidentiality program and record confidentiality rule were both found.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is from the RI legislature's compiled General Laws site, which may not yet show 2026 session laws. The rule amendment effective 10/13/2026 says it implements 2026 changes to 12-25-20 and 12-25-21.1: hit-and-run serious bodily injury added, stalking victims allowed relocation or home-modification awards, larceny and the crime against nature offenses removed from the covered list, and emergency relocation raised to $8,000. The introduced H 8155 text only changes the relocation amount; it leaves the $1,000 home-safety cap and $25,000 total cap unchanged, but the enacted version was not saved, so RI-SECURITY-1 should be rechecked once the compiled statute updates. The AG page says exam compensation is available regardless of cooperation, while 12-25-19(d)(1)(i) lets the office weigh cooperation for other awards; statute wins for non-exam expenses. The program FAQ (RI-S8) also lists a DCYF report for minors and a no contact order for domestic violence victims as alternatives to a police report. Other caps in the rule not recorded as rules: eyeglasses $200, crime scene cleanup $2,000, burial $10,000, secondary victim counseling $1,500, group therapy at 40% of the individual rate, temporary housing $150 per night for up to 10 nights within relocation. Reviewer: the AG page says exam compensation is available regardless of reporting, but 12-25-22(a) only lets the office accept an exam in place of a police report when the exam was within 15 days of the crime, and the same AG page warns that not participating in the criminal justice system will likely limit compensation eligibility. A 2022 bill (S 2374) would have barred charging the survivor for the evidentiary exam (proposed 12-28.1-6), but chapter 12-28.1 does not exist in the compiled General Laws and 23-98-5 has no billing rule, so exam_no_bill stays not_found. The home-safety $1,000 cap appears only in the statute; neither the current rule nor the 10/13/2026 rule states a dollar cap for safety modifications. How to file: the application PDF (RI-S9, retrieved from the program page's current English link) is a flat scan with no AcroForm fields (0 fields), so it is printed and filled by hand. The mail address is taken from the form, which adds '2nd Floor'; the program page gives '50 Service Ave Warwick, RI 02886' without the floor. The online portal URL (http://cvcapp.treasury.ri.gov/) is the link target behind 'here' on the program page, not visible text. The program page has an 'email us' link (crimevictims@treasury.ri.gov) for questions only; it does not say applications can be emailed, so no email submission rule was added. The rule also lets the office request a mental health treatment plan from the treating provider (2.8(A)(3)(b)); that comes from the provider, not the applicant, so it is not a required_document. Address confidentiality: the Department of State page (RI-S17) says the ACP helps victims of sexual assault, and R.I. Gen. Laws 42-164-2(1)(vii) (RI-S16) lists sexual assault (chapter 37 of title 11) as 'abuse' regardless of whether it was reported to law enforcement; 42-164-3(b) (RI-S15) requires a sworn statement that the applicant is a victim of domestic violence or abuse, so a survivor of sexual assault by a non-family member qualifies through the 'abuse' definition. Participants are certified for five years and get the Program's Providence PO Box with an identification number; the application must be mailed to Department of State, Attention: ACP, PO Box 6888, Providence, RI 02940. The AG's sexual assault bill of rights page (RI-S12) also describes the program. Record confidentiality: 2.13 of the current rule (RI-S11) and the 10/13/2026 amended rule (RI-S14, 2.13(A)) have the same text; both say the application and the notice of award or denial are public records unless otherwise provided by law, so only supporting records (medical, counseling, employment, financial, investigative) are confidential. The application's consent page (RI-S9) also says records are protected under federal confidentiality regulations and state law and cannot be disclosed without written consent except as provided by law. No separate confidentiality section was found in chapter 12-25.

coverage.notes: No minimum loss amount was found in SDCL 23A-28B or ARSD 67:55. No relocation or housing benefit was found; lodging is covered only as part of travel for treatment, court, police meetings, or funeral (ARSD 67:55:04:05(9)). Counseling has a time limit in ARSD 67:55:04:03 but no dollar cap was found. No statutory alternative to a police report for sexual assault was found; the 5-day reporting rule in SDCL 23A-28B-25(1) applies, and the application asks for a letter explaining a late report. The exam statute (SDCL 22-22-26.2) does not say whether a survivor's health insurance may be billed for the exam. The dollar limits in ARSD chapter 67:55:04 (security $500, funeral $8,000, homicide scene cleanup $1,500) can be exceeded with commission approval under ARSD 67:55:04:20, but never above the $15,000 statutory cap. No stated processing time for an initial decision was found in the apply page, application, instructions, SDCL 23A-28B, or ARSD 67:55; the only timing found is the 15 business days to send notice of the commission's final decision after an appeal hearing (ARSD 67:55:02:11), which is not an application processing time. No fax number for filing was found (the fax on the application belongs to the DPS civil rights notice). South Dakota has no substitute-address confidentiality program like Safe at Home; the Minnesota Secretary of State's national list also shows South Dakota as having no program. The only option found is the Secretary of State's Secure Active Designation under SDCL 12-4-9.2, which hides the voter registration record only. Eligibility depends on an active protection order (chapter 25-10 or 22-19A) or living in a victims' services shelter, not on the type of crime; the SOS page names rape among the circumstances it is designed for, but no quote says sexual assault survivors are eligible as such, so covers_sexual_assault is false. Forms go to the Office of the Secretary of State, Elections Division, 500 East Capitol Avenue, Suite 204, Pierre, SD 57501. SDCL 23A-28B-36 only keeps records confidential when another law or rule already protects them; it is not a blanket confidentiality rule for claims. SDCL 23A-28B-37 says hearings on an application are open to the public and the hearing record is a public record unless the commission closes the hearing, for example because a public hearing would cause trauma for the victim.

The raw HTML of the single-rule page (SD-S9) shows the digits '2' and '4' in adjacent spans with no space, so it reads as 24 months after the crime, but the text check cannot confirm it, so SD-COUNS-1 omits the number. The application does not ask for a copy of the police report or a photo ID; the program contacts law enforcement and providers itself. South Dakota has no substitute-address confidentiality program like Safe at Home; the Minnesota Secretary of State's national list also shows South Dakota as having no program. The only option found is the Secretary of State's Secure Active Designation under SDCL 12-4-9.2, which hides the voter registration record only. Eligibility depends on an active protection order (chapter 25-10 or 22-19A) or living in a victims' services shelter, not on the type of crime; the SOS page names rape among the circumstances it is designed for, but no quote says sexual assault survivors are eligible as such, so covers_sexual_assault is false. Forms go to the Office of the Secretary of State, Elections Division, 500 East Capitol Avenue, Suite 204, Pierre, SD 57501. program.program_name: Criminal Injuries Compensation Program (Criminal Injuries Compensation Fund)
program.agency: Tennessee Department of Treasury, Division of Claims and Risk Management
program.statute_citation: T.C.A. 29-13-101 to 29-13-119; forensic exams T.C.A. 29-13-118; Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0300-02-.07

coverage.notes: No security expense rule and no dollar cap on medical, relocation, or lost wages appears in T.C.A. 29-13-101 to 29-13-119 or the saved Treasury PDFs; lost wages are a rate (85 percent of average weekly wage on the workers' compensation schedule) and relocation is limited to 2 moves. The statute and the SAFE provider page do not say whether a survivor's health insurance may be billed for the forensic exam, so insurance_billing is 'unspecified'. The 15-day report to authorities is still required for compensation (good cause can excuse delay, and sexual assault is a listed good cause); no report is needed for the forensic exam alone. The program's own web page (treasury.tn.gov, a DNN page whose content sits inside a form element) could not be saved by fetch_source.py, so its statements (victim counseling covered up to the maximum, police report or other official document) are not quoted. The application is online only; there is no application PDF. Update (Oct 3, 2026): the program page was saved as TN-S15 from a plain HTTPS fetch, with text extracted without dropping the form element; the how-to-file rules quote it.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is the 2025 Tennessee Code via Justia (legislature/Lexis site not used). Total cap disagreement: T.C.A. 29-13-106(e) states $30,000 'except as provided in subsection (h)', and (h) indexes the cap to 105 percent of the national average, published by the State Treasurer on the Treasury website (not a rule, effective July 1). The Treasury's Maximum Expense Amounts PDF (June 2025) and program page list $34,100 for crimes on or after July 1, 2025, $32,900 for 7/1/24 to 6/30/25, and $32,000 for 7/1/17 to 6/30/24. Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0300-02-.07 (rev. May 2025, TN-S14) says $34,200 for crimes on or after July 1, 2025 and contains a typo ('thirty-two thousand dollars ($32,900.00)'). The program page FAQ also still says $32,900. The lower, later Treasury-published $34,100 is recorded; confirm with the program. Medical and medical-related bills are paid at 75 percent of billed charges (T.C.A. 29-13-107(7)); a provider paid 75 percent must accept it as payment in full. Forensic exam reimbursement to the provider is capped at $1,000 and is full payment (29-13-118(d)); the provider files within 1 year of the exam. The SAFE provider page says medical treatment for injury may be billed to the patient, who may then claim compensation. Cooperation with police and prosecutors is required (29-13-109(f)) with an exception when cooperation is affected by age, psychological state, fear of retaliation, or other safety concerns (29-13-103(a)(4)). An arrest or conviction is not required (29-13-109(f)). Statute 29-13-108(b) says claims are filed in person or by mail; the Treasury says to apply through its online portal (linked as 'File a Claim' on the program page). Phone 833-867-3891 is the program's; the OVC directory lists 615-741-2734 for the Division of Claims and Risk Management. Reviewer (Oct 3, 2026): T.C.A. 29-13-106(h)(4)-(5) makes the Treasurer's website publication the operative cap and says it is not a rule, which supports $34,100 over the $34,200 in Rule 0300-02-.07. The live program page checked in Chrome on Oct 3, 2026 lists $34,100 for crimes on or after July 1, 2025 and shows no separate figure for July 1, 2026, even though (h)(2) calls for an annual comparison starting January 1, 2026; if a 2026 adjustment is published later, CAP-1 needs a new source. The same page says counseling 'may be considered for the victim up to the maximum award' (not saved; fetch_source.py --chrome returned 'blocked or empty'). T.C.A. 29-13-105(c) bars an award to a victim who was a member of the offender's family only if a benefit would go to the offender, and says it does not automatically disqualify such a victim. How to file (Oct 3, 2026): the Treasury takes claims online only (resource guide TN-S1 and program page TN-S15, whose File a Claim link goes to an Origami Risk incident-entry portal); there is no paper or PDF application, so program.application_form is {source_id: null, fillable: false, field_count: 0}. T.C.A. 29-13-108(b) still says claims are filed 'in person or by mail', but no saved source gives a mailing or walk-in address for claims, so no mail or in_person submission rule was added. The only address published is on the Employer's Statement (TN-S16, RDA-1178, a fillable PDF with 60 AcroForm fields): 502 Deaderick Street, Nashville, TN 37243-0202, where the employer sends that form. The online form must be finished in one session; supporting documents are uploaded as PDF or Word files. Criminal.Injury@tn.gov is published for advocates, not as a claim submission address. TN-S15 was saved by hand because fetch_source.py strips form elements and this DNN page sits inside one; raw bytes are the server's HTML and the sha256 matches. Address confidentiality: Tennessee's program is Safe at Home, run by the Secretary of State under T.C.A. 40-38-601 to 40-38-614 (statute calls it the address confidentiality program). 40-38-602(a) opens it to victims of rape, sexual battery, or another sexual offense at no cost; 40-38-602(b) gives a substitute address and bars disclosure of the participant's file; 40-38-602(f) and (j) make the participant's file and application not public records. The substitute address may not be used for property tax or recorded real property documents (40-38-602(d)). Registered sex, animal abuse, vulnerable-adult abuse, and drug offenders are ineligible (40-38-603). Under 40-38-604(a)-(b) the application is filed with an application assistant and needs either documentary evidence of a criminal case, an order of protection in effect, or a notarized statement from a licensed professional (attorney, social worker, therapist) that the applicant is in danger, plus a sworn statement, notarized signatures, and an address not in any public record or a move within 30 days before or 90 days after applying. A survivor who has not reported can still qualify through the professional's statement. Record confidentiality: T.C.A. 10-7-504(k) closes only four items about compensation applicants to the public (residential address, home and personal cell numbers, SSN, and the offense being compensated); the victim's name and other claim contents are not listed there, and no confidentiality section was found in T.C.A. 29-13-101 to 29-13-119. The Comptroller's 2018 list of Public Records Act exceptions (TN-S22) lists 10-7-504(k) as the Criminal Injuries Compensation Act exception.
