program.agency: Office of the Attorney General of Texas, Crime Victim Services Division
program.statute_citation: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. ch. 56B; forensic exams under ch. 56A, subch. G (arts. 56A.301 to 56A.309); 1 Tex. Admin. Code ch. 61

coverage.notes: No minimum loss requirement appears in Chapter 56B or the program pages I saved. I found no statute, rule, or program page that covers home security devices, so security is left out. The statute does not say whether a survivor's own insurance may be billed for the forensic portion of the exam, so insurance_billing is unspecified. Travel has no dollar cap of its own: 1 TAC 61.404(c) limits transportation, meals, and lodging to the maximum rates for Texas state employees, which I did not encode as a number. No processing time is stated: the How to Apply page says processing time varies for each case.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is from statutes.capitol.texas.gov (current through the 89th Legislature, 2nd Called Session, 2025). Administrative rules (1 TAC ch. 61) are from Cornell LII because the Texas SOS site is hard to snapshot; those rules still cite the pre-2021 article numbers (art. 56.32, 56.42) from before Chapter 56 was recodified into 56A/56B, so check them against the SOS Texas Administrative Code before relying on them for edge cases. Filing deadline: the statute (art. 56B.052) says the third anniversary of the crime; I quoted the program page because it states the 3 years numerically. For a child victim the statute runs 3 years from when the claimant is made aware of the offense but not after the child turns 21 (art. 56B.052(c)); periods of crime-caused incapacity are excluded (art. 56B.052(d)). Sexual assault Emergency Medical Care (EMC) compensation under art. 56A.305 is separate from the $50,000 aggregate cap (the OAG medical care page says an additional $25,000 may be available) and does not need a police report; EMC applications must be filed within 3 years of the exam per the OAG EMC page. Counseling: 1 TAC 61.503 says 60 sessions for conduct after September 1, 2014 while the OAG page says after 8/31/2014; the program page also says compensation is generally one session per week. Catastrophic injuries resulting in total and permanent disability can get up to $75,000 more (art. 56B.106(b)); not encoded as a rule. Relocation: the $5,000 cap in art. 56B.106(c-3) applies to crimes after 8/31/2023 per the OAG page; earlier crimes had different limits. The program allows one move, within 3 years of the crime. The paper application PDF (TX-S16) is dated 10/15 and cites the old Chapter 56; the online portal is the program's preferred route. Reviewer: the 1 TAC ch. 61 copies on Cornell LII show no amendments after 2017, and the OAG pages agree with the 60-session counseling limit and the $700 weekly lost-wage limit; the $300 weekly childcare, $2250 crime scene cleanup and $1000 seized-property limits are confirmed only by the TAC text. The EMC $25,000 applies to exams after August 31, 2023 per the OAG EMC page, and the 30-day follow-up coverage applies to care sought after August 31, 2025. Filing: the paper application (TX-S16, rev. 10/15, 245 AcroForm fields) is still the one linked from the How to Apply page, which also links a Spanish version. It says to mail it to the OAG CVC Program (011), P.O. Box 12198, Austin, Texas 78711-2198; the newer program pages give the same P.O. box addressed to Crime Victim Services. The online target URL (https://cvs.texasattorneygeneral.gov/portal/login) is the href of the 'Sign In to the CVC Portal' link on TX-S5; the URL itself is not in the page text. Documents sent after applying can go through the portal, the CVC Documentation Upload webform, or by mail. The application says not to wait for documents before mailing it. No fax, email, or in-person filing route is stated; the program says it does not routinely communicate with victims by email. Privacy: the Address Confidentiality Program is in Tex. Code Crim. Proc. ch. 58, subch. B (arts. 58.051 and following), run by the OAG; art. 58.052(a) lists victims of sexual assault or abuse, and the OAG ACP page (TX-S23) gives the application steps, says applicants not working with an advocate need a protective order, restraining order or injunction, or documentation of the crime, and says enrollment lasts 3 years at a time with renewal. Art. 58.053 requires state and local agencies to accept the substitute address, with exemptions set by OAG rule. Compensation records: art. 56B.058(c) lists the exceptions for release (court order for good cause, consent of the claimant or victim, and others), and a subpoena response releases only the completed application with Gov. Code 552.132(b) confidential information redacted (art. 56B.058(d)).

program.agency: Utah Office for Victims of Crime (UOVC)
program.statute_citation: Utah Code 75E-5-101 to 75E-5-314 (formerly 63M-7-501 to 63M-7-525); Utah Admin. Code R270-1

coverage.notes: No filing deadline appears in Utah Code 75E-5 (effective 7/1/2026), in R270-1, on the program pages, or on the application; the closest rules are R270-1-23 (a claim expires three years after the date of application, extendable for extenuating circumstances) and R270-1-24(5) (exam reimbursement requests are due within one year of the exam), neither of which is a deadline for a victim to apply. R270-1-9(1)(b) says no time limit is required for filing an emergency claim. No minimum loss amount was found. No rule names phones or other ordinary property as excluded; the statute covers only personal property necessary and essential to health or safety (75E-5-309(1)(d)(viii)), and the program page says property crimes are not eligible crimes. Neither the statute nor R270-1-24 says whether the survivor's own insurance may be billed for the exam; the UOVC sexual assault provider billing page says providers must bill all available insurance before billing UOVC, so insurance_billing is left unspecified. Privacy (added Oct 3): Safe at Home was recodified from Title 77, Chapter 38, Part 6 to Title 75E, Chapter 11 (Chapter 291, 2026 General Session, effective 7/1/2026); the Title 77 Part 6 page now holds only 77-38-6.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Utah recodified the Crime Victim Reparations Act from Title 63M, Chapter 7, Part 5 into Title 75E, Chapter 5 (Chapter 291, 2026 General Session, effective 7/1/2026). R270-1 (effective 12/08/2023, continuation notice March 6, 2026) still cites the old 63M-7 section numbers, and the application PDF still cites 63M-7-519 and 63M-7-510. The rule-based caps (relocation $2,000, transportation $1,000, essential property $1,500/$5,000, emergency $1,000, 25 counseling sessions, 12 weeks lost earnings) come from R270-1 and the board may approve more in extenuating circumstances. The UOVC Code R payment table (UT-S6) lists $625 for an exam and $1250 with photo documentation for dates of service from January 5, 2023; R270-1-24 sets the $1,250 maximum with photo documentation. 75E-5-313(2) also bars medical providers from debt collection while a claim is pending (summarized on the FAQ, UT-S2). Phone 801-238-2360 matches the OVC directory; toll free 1-800-621-7444 is on the application. Online application: https://newclaim.crimevictim.utah.gov/ . Reviewer: R270-1-24(1)(a)'s $1,250 is the examiner fee only (the Code R table, UT-S6, lists $625 without photo documentation), and the facility is paid separately under R270-1-24(2), so it is recorded as exam_payment, not as a survivor-facing expense cap. insurance_billing is set to allowed because the UOVC provider billing page (UT-S4) requires providers to bill all available insurance before UOVC; neither the statute nor R270-1-24 addresses it directly. R270-1-24(3) conditions provider reimbursement on the provider reporting the exam to law enforcement and collecting evidence only with the victim's permission; this is a provider condition, not a survivor reporting requirement. R270-1-8 (abortion) cites 63M-7-511, now 75E-5-309, and is limited to abortions permitted under Title 76, Chapter 7, Part 3. 75E-5-313(1)(b) lets a medical provider (not the exam provider, which R270-1-24(6) covers) collect from the victim up to the office's rate if the office cannot pay in full. How to file (added Oct 3): UOVC moved. The contact page (UT-S9, modified 2026-06-30) and the UOVC homepage list 420 East South Temple, Suite 500, Salt Lake City, UT 84111, while the application PDF (UT-S5, same file as live, created Jan 2025) and the provider billing page (UT-S4) still print 350 East 500 South Suite 200; the submission rule uses the newer contact-page address. Fax 801-533-4127 is the same on both. The online portal URL comes from the apply page's Online Application link, not its visible text. The FAQ (UT-S2) says to send claim correspondence to the program email, which the saved text shows as Cloudflare-obfuscated; the decoded address in the HTML is crimevictims@utah.gov, matching the application, so UT-SUBMIT-2 quotes the application header. The application has 90 AcroForm fields. No in-person submission method is stated. UT-DOC-7 is stored under funeral but the quote covers relocation costs too. Privacy (added Oct 3): UT-ACP-1 quotes the Safe at Home homepage (UT-S11). The statute, now Utah Code Title 75E, Chapter 11 (UT-S16, renumbered from 77-38-601 et seq. by Chapter 291, 2026 General Session), creates the program 'within the department' (75E-11-102(1)), and 75E-1-101(2) (UT-S17) defines the department as the Department of Criminal Justice; the program site carries that department's logo. The statute's definition of victim covers a sexual offense under Title 76, Chapter 5, Part 4, and 75E-11-302 requires a program assistant's recommendation, a relocation within 90 days or an address unknown to the assailant, and does not require a police report or criminal charge. The enroll text is from the How to Enroll page (UT-S13), which also lists program assistants by county; those names are not recorded here. UT-RECCONF-1 quotes 75E-5-205(1); 75E-5-205(6) also requires the office to redact the name of a sexual assault victim and claimant contact information before releasing any restitution record. UT-S15 (Utah Code 77-38-6, a victim's right to withhold locating information in court and use initials in public criminal justice documents) was saved while locating the Safe at Home statute and is not cited by a rule.

jurisdictions.name: Virginia

program.program_name: Virginia Victims Fund (Criminal Injuries Compensation Fund)
program.agency: Virginia Workers' Compensation Commission

not_found: expense_cap counseling for direct victims (no dollar cap found in statute or program pages)
expense_cap medical (no separate cap found; only the $35,000 total)
expense_cap transportation (mileage covered only for minor victims; no rate found)
expense_cap temporary_housing dollar amount (only a 30-day limit found)
administrative code rules setting caps (none found; caps are in statute and VVF policy)

expense_cap lost_wages (the statute sets no maximum weekly amount for total loss of earnings; the $600 per week figure limits actual earnings plus partial-loss compensation combined, so it was not recorded as a cap)
processing_time (no official source states a time for a decision or payment)
coverage.notes: Exam payment is the SAFE Payment Program run by the Virginia Victims Fund under Va. Code § 19.2-368.11:1(F) and § 19.2-165.1(B). The claimant/victim FAQ page (vvf.virginia.gov/claimant-victim-faqs) could not be saved by the fetch tool and was not used. The VVF Policies PDF (Sept 2025) references an Available Benefits section that is not in the published PDF.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text retrieved Oct 3 2026 reflects 2025 and 2026 amendments: total cap $35,000 (§ 19.2-368.11:1(H)) and a three-year filing deadline (§ 19.2-368.5(B)). VVF pages say the three-year deadline applies to crimes on or after July 1, 2025 and that caps follow the policy in effect on the date of the crime, so older crimes may fall under a one-year deadline and older caps. Disagreement: the statute caps survivor counseling for family of homicide victims at $3,500 per claim (§ 19.2-368.11:1(E)(v)), while the VVF eligibility page and claim form list grief counseling up to $5,000; neither cap applies to direct sexual assault victims, so no counseling cap was recorded. Disagreement: the VVF Policies PDF says only victims of child sexual assault are exempt from prompt reporting, but the current § 19.2-368.10(3) says the reporting subdivision does not apply to claims of sexual abuse, which § 19.2-368.2 defines to include adult rape, sodomy, object sexual penetration and sexual battery; the statute controls. For other crimes, prompt reporting is judged from police records, the victim's situation, and any permanent protective order (§ 19.2-368.10(3)); the claim form says crimes between July 1, 1998 and June 30, 2025 used a 120-hour reporting standard with good cause. Once a claim is filed, notified health care providers must stop debt collection until a decision (§ 19.2-368.5:2). SAFE provider reimbursement rates (60% of eligible charges for acute exams, $1,500 non-acute, $1,000 follow-up) are payments to providers, not survivor caps, and were not recorded as rules. Lost wages for direct victims are paid at two-thirds of average weekly wage; the $600 weekly figure applies to partial loss of earnings combined with actual earnings. Reviewer: removed the $600 per week lost_wages expense_cap because it limits combined earnings plus partial-loss compensation, not the benefit itself, and would understate total-loss benefits; the statute text is § 19.2-368.11:1(B). VVF says caps follow the policy in effect on the date of the crime, so older crimes may fall under different caps that are not recorded here. How to file: the claim form (VA-S11, 08/12/2025, the version linked from the VVF Claim Form page, 175 AcroForm fields) says to submit by mail to P.O. Box 26927, Richmond, VA 23261 or fax 804-823-6905; § 19.2-368.5(C) and the VVF Policies also allow in-person filing, and the contact page says in-person assistance is by appointment only (appointment@vvf.virginia.gov). There is no public online application: WebFile is for trained victim advocates and medical providers, so a survivor who wants to file electronically goes through a local Victim/Witness program. Disagreement: the VVF Policies PDF (Sept 2025) says supporting documents can be e-mailed to info@virginiavictimsfund.org, but the newer Contact Us page says VVF is no longer accepting documents via email for security reasons, so no email submission rule was recorded. SAFE exam submission targets (fax 804-823-6907, safe@vvf.virginia.gov) are for providers and were not recorded as survivor filing methods. No processing time is stated; the only time limits are on the claimant (180 days after the acknowledgement letter to send requested documents, and two years from eligibility per the How Compensation Works page). Privacy: Virginia's Address Confidentiality Program (Va. Code § 2.2-515.2) is run by the Office of the Attorney General; 'sexual violence' is defined to include rape (§ 18.2-61) and other sexual offenses, regardless of whether the conduct was reported or charged. Applicants must be at least 18 (or a parent/guardian for a minor or incapacitated person, or an emancipated minor), apply in person through an accredited sexual or domestic violence program or a crime victim and witness assistance program, are certified for three years, and residents of temporary housing for 30 days or less cannot enroll until they have a permanent address. Participants can ask any state or local agency to use the designated address, and ACP records identifying participants are exempt from Virginia FOIA (§ 2.2-515.2(G)). Record confidentiality comes from the VVF Confidentiality page, not a statute: no statute was found that makes compensation claim files confidential as a whole; § 19.2-368.3(2) (VA-S20) only makes investigative information the Commission obtains from police, prosecutors and the medical examiner confidential. The VVF page also notes that the signed Notarized Agreement lets VVF share information with agencies, providers, employers and insurers to decide eligibility.

jurisdictions.name: Vermont

program.agency: Vermont Center for Crime Victim Services (Victims Compensation Board)

not_found: expense_cap for medical (no dollar cap; uninsured providers paid 60 percent of billed charges)
coverage.notes: No minimum loss was found in the statute, the Board rule, or the program pages. No dollar cap for security expenses was found. The emergency advance comes from the Board's administrative rule; no amount is set there. No processing time is stated; the FAQ says approval time depends on how long it takes to verify the losses.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Vermont runs two paths: Victims Compensation under 13 V.S.A. ch. 167 (police report concluding a crime occurred is required by 13 V.S.A. 5353(a)(1)), and the CCVS Sexual Assault Program under 32 V.S.A. 1407, which pays exam costs and follow-up counseling with no police report, only a report to a medical provider. The CCVS Application & Forms page says applicants do not have to provide a police report; I read that as not having to attach a copy (the claims specialist gathers it), not as waiving the statutory report requirement. Exam billing: 1407(c) requires providers to bill the survivor's insurance first, so insurance_billing is 'allowed' (in fact required); the survivor owes nothing because the Fund pays cost-sharing and providers cannot balance bill uninsured survivors. Filing deadline: the statute ties the deadline to the prosecution limitation period; 13 V.S.A. 4501(a) has no limit for sexual assault and aggravated sexual assault, but other sex offenses in 4501(b)-(e) have limits, so VT-DEADLINE-2 only covers the crimes it lists. Counseling and lost-wage figures are CCVS policies with effective dates: counseling $100/session applies to services from August 12, 2024; lost wages $750/week applies to claims filed on or after 9/8/2025 (older claims $500/week). The Board administrative rule (Code Vt. R. 80-220-001, via Cornell LII) lists older internal caps (mental health $3,000, lost wages $1,500, temporary living $1,500/month) that conflict with the current CCVS policies; I did not encode those caps and only used the rule for the emergency advance and transportation-for-treatment provisions. Relocation caps are stated in the policy without a per-claim unit; the policy says relocation is generally paid no more than once in 12 months. Reviewer: VT-TRAVEL-1's $2,000 cap applies only to travel to court proceedings, Parole Board hearings, and pre-sentence investigations in non-homicide cases (plus $2,000 more per separately tried defendant); it is not a cap on travel to medical or counseling treatment (VT-TRAVEL-2). The Board rule (VT-S16) is an old version (it lists a Montpelier address and a 7-digit phone) and is used only for the emergency advance and treatment transportation. How to file: the English application (VT-S8, last modified 8/13/2024, the version linked from the Application & Forms page) is a fillable PDF with 180 AcroForm fields. It can be mailed or filed online at ccvcvt.org (VT-S18). The application's cover page lists 58 South Main Street, Suite One, Waterbury, Vermont 05676-1599, but the online portal and the 2026 policy letterheads list 60 South Main Street, Suite 1, Waterbury, VT 05676(-1599); the mail rule keeps the application's address verbatim, and Tend should show the newer one alongside it. A fax number (802-241-1253, Victims Compensation only) is printed on the application and policies, but no source says the application can be faxed, so I did not add a fax submission rule. The Application & Forms page says applicants do not have to provide a police report, so police_report is not a required document. The Sexual Assault Program path (exam and counseling, no police report) does not use the compensation application; the signed Sexual Assault Billing Form from the SANE visit opens the claim. Privacy: Vermont's address confidentiality program is Safe at Home, run by the Secretary of State under 15 V.S.A. §§ 1150 to 1160 (VT-S20). The statute lists sexual assault victims as eligible (15 V.S.A. § 1152(a)(1)(A)(i)) and says applications are filed directly with the Secretary's office or through a certified applicant assistant (§ 1152(b)); certification lasts four years (§ 1152(c)). The SOS page (VT-S19) says the program is a mail forwarding service with a Montpelier post office box as the substitute address, and it does not protect land records in real estate transactions. Record confidentiality: 13 V.S.A. § 5358a(a) makes the Board's application documents confidential; § 5358a(c) also requires the Board to redact the victim's residential address, phone, other contact information, and Social Security number for any purpose including restitution, and in sexual offense cases keeps the victim's employer and medical or mental health provider contact information confidential absent a court order.

jurisdictions.name: Washington

program.agency: Washington State Department of Labor & Industries
program.statute_citation: Chapter 7.68 RCW (RCW 7.68.170 for exam costs); chapter 296-30 WAC

not_found: reporting_requirement alternatives for sexual assault (compensation claims)
coverage.notes: No emergency or advance award, minimum loss, relocation, or security benefit was found in chapter 7.68 RCW, chapter 296-30 WAC, or the L&I program pages that were saved. For compensation claims the crime must be reported to law enforcement within 12 months (RCW 7.68.060(1)(b)); no sexual-assault alternative to a police report was found for compensation claims. The police report is not required for the sexual assault exam itself, which the program pays for directly (RCW 7.68.170, WAC 296-30-170). Mental health sessions beyond the first six need prior authorization per the Mental Health Fee Schedule (F800-105-000); that is an authorization step, not a dollar cap, so it is not encoded as a rule. Reviewer changes (Oct 3): the $40,000 limit in RCW 7.68.070(1) applies to all non-medical benefits, so it is encoded as an expense_cap (expense "other") instead of a second total_cap; the only total_cap is the L&I per-claim maximum of $190,000. The 60 percent wage rule is a covered_expense note, not a dollar cap. Exam payment does not apply when the victim was confined in a jail or institution at the time of the assault (F800-100-000). HIV PEP (up to a 28-day supply from a WA hospital ED) is covered. Minor victims of sex trafficking or commercial sexual abuse of a minor may apply at any time (RCW 7.68.060(6)(b)). Privacy (Oct 3): RCW 7.68.140 makes victim claim files and records confidential and not open to public inspection, with exceptions for public employees doing official duties, a claimant's signed authorization, treating or advising physicians, and others assisting the department. The Secretary of State runs the Address Confidentiality Program under chapter 40.24 RCW; survivors of sexual assault are eligible.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Federal OVC directory lists the WA compensation program as the Department of Labor & Industries, phone 800-762-3716, website lni.wa.gov/claims/crime-victim-claims/apply-for-crime-victim-benefits. The L&I apply page said on Oct 3, 2026 that the online application portal was down and to email or fax the PDF form. Cap structure: RCW 7.68.070(1) caps non-medical benefits at $40,000 per injury, and RCW 7.68.085 separately caps medical benefits at $150,000; the L&I page states the combined per-claim maximum as $190,000 and groups medical and mental health under the $150,000. The burial cap in statute ($6,170) is inflation-adjusted every three years and the L&I page shows $7,990; funeral is not encoded. The minor filing rule (within two years of the 18th birthday) comes from the L&I page; it was not found in the text of RCW 7.68.060, which instead has a discovery rule for adult victims of childhood crimes. Exam insurance billing is marked unspecified: RCW 7.68.170 bars billing or charging the victim directly or indirectly and WAC 296-30-170 makes the program the primary payer, and the L&I page says patients are not required to use their own insurance, but no source expressly says whether a provider may bill the survivor's insurer. RCW 7.68.060(2)(a) consent/provocation/incitement is a full eligibility bar, not a reduction; it is recorded as conduct_reduction for information only. RCW 7.68.080 has a version effective until June 30, 2027 and one effective June 30, 2027; the quoted subsections read the same in both. Reviewer: RCW 7.68.060(1)(a) also says the 3-year clock runs from the report date; the L&I minors rule (two years after the 18th birthday) is not in RCW 7.68.060 and may come from a rule or policy that was not saved, so treat it as agency guidance. The exam billing manual (F800-100-000) calls the program the primary payer for the initial exam and covers prophylaxis, emergency contraception, hepatitis B immune globulin, tetanus vaccine, and up to 28 days of HIV medication with the exam; treatment of injuries needs a compensation application. How-to-file (Oct 3): the injury application F800-042-000 (07-2017, saved as WA-S15) is the current version linked from the L&I apply and forms pages; it has 112 AcroForm fields over 5 pages. The apply page says the online portal is down for repair, so no online submission rule is encoded; the page says to email or fax the PDF instead, and its FAQ says printed applications can go by mail or fax. The mail rule uses the PO Box printed on the form. The police report and medical reports come from the FAQ about sending supporting documentation (write the claim number on each page); no source lists a full checklist of attachments. Address confidentiality (Oct 3): the Washington ACP is run by the Secretary of State under chapter 40.24 RCW. RCW 40.24.030 (WA-S23) requires a sworn statement that the applicant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, trafficking, or stalking and fears for their safety. Applicants enroll through a designated Application Assistant at an advocacy agency, who forwards the application; the Application Process page (WA-S25) says certified participants are enrolled for four years and get an authorization card. The enroll param is copied as written on the ACP page, including its typo ("completing and application"). The first URL tried for the ACP page returned a 404, so WA-S24 was re-saved from the correct statewide-programs URL. Record confidentiality: RCW 7.68.140 (WA-S22).

jurisdictions.name: Wisconsin

program.agency: Wisconsin Department of Justice, Office of Crime Victim Services
program.statute_citation: Wis. Stat. ch. 949, subch. I (ss. 949.001 to 949.18); SAFE Fund: subch. II (ss. 949.20 to 949.38); Wis. Admin. Code ch. Jus 11

not_found: reporting alternatives for sexual assault (compensation claims)
coverage.notes: No minimum loss amount appears in current Wis. Stat. ch. 949 or Jus 11. No emergency or advance award provision was found (the FAQ mentions only that 'Some exceptions may be made for emergency situations' when waiting on insurance or lawsuits). No relocation, temporary housing, or home security expense category was found; 'securing' a crime scene is part of the $1,000 crime scene cleanup cap, not personal security. The FAQ says mileage for appointments and court is not paid; no covered transportation rule was found. No separate cap on the victim's own counseling or lost wages was found beyond the $40,000 total. For compensation claims, the police report rule (5 days, waivable in the interest of justice) has no sexual-assault-specific alternative in the statute or rules; the forensic exam itself is paid by the SAFE Fund with no report required. Address confidentiality: Safe at Home (Wis. Stat. 165.68) is run by the Department of Justice; 165.68(1)(a)3. counts sexual abuse as defined in 103.10(1m)(b)6., which covers violations of s. 940.225 (sexual assault), so covers_sexual_assault is true. Record confidentiality: 949.05(2)(a) shields applicant PII only for claims from listed sexual offenses; 949.16 otherwise says the record of a proceeding is a public record.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text is the LRB 2023-24 Wis. Stats. PDF published 10-1-26 (updated through 2025 Wis. Act 247). Jus 11 is the Register November 2024 PDF; its text extraction renders curly quotes and apostrophes as X/Y/[ so quotes from it avoid those characters. The wisdoj.gov SharePoint pages wrap the whole body in a <form>, which the standard fetch tool strips, so WI-S3 to WI-S7 were saved with the same plain HTTP fetch and the same text extraction except that form content is kept; raw HTML and sha256 are the real bytes. Those pages contain zero-width spaces, so quotes were chosen from spans without them. SAFE Fund provider reimbursement is two-thirds of billed eligible services up to $1,200 per exam in Jus 11.16(4), inflation-adjusted yearly; the SAFE Fund page lists the current maximum as $1,621.22. That limit is on the provider's reimbursement, not on the survivor; the no-bill rule in 949.26(2)(a) applies to providers who seek a SAFE Fund award. The SAFE Fund page says it can reimburse when a victim does not want to report, cooperate, or bill insurance. Older DOJ addresses (doj.state.wi.us) still appear on the application PDF; the program phone 800-446-6564 matches the OVC directory and the program page. 949.08(2)(a) bars rather than reduces an award for contributing conduct, and does not apply to people injured aiding victims or police. Reviewer: 949.26(1m) bars a SAFE Fund award when the provider is authorized to bill insurance and the victim cooperates with law enforcement, so the SAFE Fund no-bill rule in 949.26(2) is tied to providers seeking a fund award; a survivor who reports and authorizes insurance billing falls outside it (CVC awards are then reduced by any SAFE award under 949.06(3)(f)). The SAFE Fund pays the provider two-thirds of billed eligible services up to the yearly cap, and the provider may not bill the survivor for the rest. 949.06(4)(a) also says an award may be made whether or not anyone is prosecuted or convicted. How to file: the application page (WI-S5) lists online (recommended) and mail or fax for the paper form. The paper application (WI-S8, DJ-CVC-1 Rev. 10/2024, byte-identical to the live PDF on Oct 3 2026) has no AcroForm fields, so it is print-and-fill only. Its return block also lists Email: ocvs@doj.state.wi.us and the old www.doj.state.wi.us domain; the current pages list ocvs@wisdoj.gov only as a contact address and say paper applications may be mailed or faxed, so no email submission rule was added. The FAQ says nothing has to be sent with the application (bills are optional at filing and the program follows up), and police reports are requested by the program directly from law enforcement, so no police_report document rule was added. No photo ID or proof of residency requirement was found. Processing time is the intake estimate on the program page (90-120 days or longer); no statutory decision deadline was recorded. Privacy (added Oct 3 2026): WI-ACP-1 quotes the DOJ Safe at Home page (WI-S9), saved with the same form-preserving plain HTTP fetch as WI-S3 to WI-S7 because the standard tool strips the SharePoint <form> body; the quote avoids the zero-width spaces on that page. The governing statute is Wis. Stat. 165.68 (WI-S10): eligibility requires Wisconsin residency and being a victim of abuse (or fearing for physical safety), 'Abuse' includes 'Sexual abuse, as defined in s. 103.10 (1m) (b) 6.', and that definition (WI-S11) lists s. 940.225, the sexual assault statute. Participation lasts 5 years and the department may not charge a fee. The enroll text is copied from WI-S9. WI-RECCONF-1 is narrow: 949.05(2)(a) exempts applicant personally identifiable information from public inspection and copying only when the claim arises from s. 940.22(2), 940.225, 948.02, 948.025, 948.051, 948.085, 948.095 or a sexually motivated crime; for other claims 949.16 says 'The record of a proceeding before an examiner or the department under this subchapter is a public record', with records confidential under other law staying confidential. The SAFE Fund has its own rule (949.36): the victim's PII stays confidential when a provider seeks an award unless the victim consents in writing.

jurisdictions.name: West Virginia

program.agency: West Virginia Legislative Claims Commission
program.statute_citation: W. Va. Code 14-2A-1 to 14-2A-29; forensic exam payment at W. Va. Code 61-8B-16

coverage.notes: No minimum loss amount appears in the statute or program pages (the old eligibility page only says there must be an economic loss). No emergency or advance award provision was found in W. Va. Code 14-2A. No dollar cap for the victim's own counseling, lost wages or medical care was found beyond the $35,000 total; the only counseling cap found is $5,000 for secondary victims (14-2A-3(a)(5)), which is not encoded as a rule because it does not apply to the survivor. Security devices and temporary housing are not listed as allowable expenses. The program may set maximum rates for health care services by rule or order (14-2A-19b), but no rate schedule was found. Record confidentiality is limited: 14-2A-11a(b) makes Fund records confidential only for claims filed on behalf of a minor child who is the subject of a civil abuse and neglect petition; nothing in 14-2A, the program's procedural rules, or the program pages makes an adult survivor's claim confidential.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statutes were read from code.wvlegislature.gov on 2026-10-03 (14-2A-3 shows 2025 amendments). Program pages disagree with the statute in places, and the statute is used: (1) the older eligibility page at wvlegislature.gov/Joint/Victims/eligibility.cfm and the application packet say a report within 72 hours, while 14-2A-14(b) now says 96 hours and accepts a forensic exam for sexual offenses; the newer victims.wvlegislature.gov eligibility page matches the statute. (2) Program pages list funeral costs up to $7,000 or $10,000; the statute says $10,000 (not encoded since it only applies to death claims). (3) Both eligibility pages say a minor victim must file before the 20th birthday, but 14-2A-10(b) as read only states two years from the crime; WV-DEAD-2 shows the Fund page's rule in its own words, as the Fund's statement, and the engine stays statute-only. Other notes: 14-2A-18 makes the filing of criminal charges a prerequisite with exceptions (unknown offender, juvenile claimant, or adult who did not block charges where law enforcement confirms a crime occurred). 14-2A-19b says a provider that accepts the commission's payment must take it as payment in full and may not bill the claimant the difference. Program Rule 12 says the commission pays medical providers 50% of outstanding balances after collateral sources as payment in full, with no reduction against the claimant. 14-2A-14(g)(2) allows up to $100,000 more for special needs when the injury leaves the victim disabled under the Social Security Act. Claims close 10 years after filing or when benefits run out (14-2A-14a). Toll-free number 1-877-562-6878 (within West Virginia) is on WV-S8. A secondary eligibility page lists (304) 347-4851, which looks like a typo; the phone uses 304-347-4850 from the home page and the OVC directory. Reviewer: 14-2A-14(a) opens with "Except as provided in §14-2A-10(b)", which hints at an exception to the two-year limit, but the saved 14-2A-10(b) (last amended 2017) states no exception; the program's minor-victim rule (file before the 20th birthday) could not be tied to statute text and stays out of the rules. WV-REP-2 is a criminal-charge requirement (14-2A-18), stricter than a police report; the engine should not treat it as satisfied by a forensic exam. The court-travel cap in WV-CAP-3 does not apply to medical travel. How to file (added 2026-10-03): the application PDF (WV-S11, last modified 2016 and still the file linked from the program home page) is a flat, non-fillable form with 0 AcroForm fields, so it is printed and filled by hand. Its cover page says to mail it to the Fund; the home page (WV-S8) also links an online claim form (WV-S12, saved directly because the page text is short and the fetch tool's length check flagged it). The packet and home page list a fax number (304-347-4915) and email (cvictims@wvlegislature.gov) as contact details only, never as ways to file, so no fax or email submission rule is encoded; because the release must be notarized, the survivor should mail the original. Rule 4 says the application is filed in duplicate while the packet does not mention copies; WV-DOC-4 records the rule. Death-claim documents (death certificate, funeral bills, guardianship papers) are listed on the form but not encoded since they do not apply to a surviving victim. Processing times come from the procedural rules (6 months for the investigator's finding, then a 30-day response window, then 45 days for the Commissioner's opinion); no program page gives an overall decision or payment time. The victims.wvlegislature.gov application link (/crime-victims-compensation-application/) returned 404 on 2026-10-03. Privacy (added 2026-10-03): The Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Secretary of State under W. Va. Code 48-28A. 48-28A-101 (WV-S14) names victims of sexual assault, and the SOS page (WV-S16) lists sexual assault among eligibility grounds; it also requires having relocated within 30 days or planning to relocate, no government records at the new address, West Virginia residency, and age 18 or a parent or guardian applying for a minor. 48-28A-103 (WV-S15) says applications go through an application assistant and certification lasts four years. The ACP contact line (866) 767-8683 and acp@wvsos.gov are on WV-S16. For compensation records, I read every section of 14-2A on code.wvlegislature.gov. The only confidentiality provision is 14-2A-11a(b), which covers claims for a minor child in a civil abuse and neglect case (WV-RECCONF-1 is scoped to that). 14-2A-12(c) lets a court issue protective orders over police and prosecutor records the claim investigator requests, which protects witnesses but does not make the claim itself confidential, so it is not encoded. 14-2A-21 requires an annual public report listing the amount of each award. The engine should not tell an adult survivor in West Virginia that the claim file is confidential by law.

jurisdictions.name: Wyoming

program.agency: Wyoming Office of the Attorney General, Division of Victim Services

not_found: temporary_housing (beyond per diem lodging during relocation and travel)
dollar cap on lost wages (paid at federal minimum wage for up to 3 months instead)
administrative rules text (DVS rules, Chapter 3) not saved
a no-bill rule for anonymous exams (policy says DVS pays, but does not say the survivor may not be billed)
address_confidentiality (Wyoming has no state address confidentiality program)
coverage.notes: No minimum loss amount appears in the statute, guidelines, FAQ, or instructions. Catastrophic injury can add up to $10,000 on top of the $15,000 maximum under W.S. 1-40-109(e); it is not encoded as a rule because it applies only to permanent disability. The guidelines also set a $3,000 counseling limit for elderly victims of financial fraud, not encoded because it does not apply to sexual assault. The exam no-bill rules come from the program's policy document, not from statute; W.S. 6-2-309(g) only says who pays. Wyoming has no address confidentiality (Safe at Home) program: no statute, Secretary of State page, or Attorney General page for one turned up, the Arizona Secretary of State's national ACP list (azsos.gov, ACP_Throughout_the_United_States.pdf) says "Wyoming. No program.", and a national ACP list from NOVA leaves Wyoming out.

jurisdictions.researcher_notes: Statute text for 1-40-106, 1-40-109, 1-40-110, 1-40-111 and 6-2-309 is from Justia's 2025 Wyoming Statutes because wyoleg.gov publishes the code as whole-title PDFs; it matches the DVS-posted copy of the Act (WY-S4), which I used for 1-40-102 definitions. Program documents (guidelines, FAQ, application, instructions) are Google Drive files linked from dvs.wyo.gov/compensation; source URLs are the direct-download form of those Drive links. The posted application is labeled SAMPLE; the program says to apply through a local victim service provider, so apply_url points to the provider list. The guidelines allow an order of protection in place of a police report for counseling-only claims, which goes beyond the statute's notification requirement in 1-40-106(a)(iv); both are recorded. Reported-exam payment by DVS is contingent on available funding under 6-2-309(g); if division funds run out, the investigating law enforcement agency pays. The guidelines say lost-wage coverage needs the victim to have been employed at the time of the crime. Reviewer: the guidelines set three relocation limits ($1,200 per claim; $500 for moving within the community; $500 when the crime scene was the home and returning would do greater harm). The application instructions (WY-S6) say relocation applies only when the crime scene was the victim's home (domestic violence, homicide, sexual assault), so for a sexual assault at home the $500 limit is the likely one. The reported-exam no-bill policy sits under a heading for reports made without a compensation claim; DVS pays only SANE exam and evidence collection costs there. How to file: the posted Primary Victim Application (WY-S5, rev. 4/23, labeled SAMPLE) is a flat PDF with no form fields, so it is printed and filled by hand. The only submission method the sources state is mail to DVS in Cheyenne (the 'Return to' line on the authorization page). The fax number and email on the letterhead are contact details, not stated filing methods, so they are not encoded. The compensation page (WY-S1) says local victim service providers give out the application, help fill it in, and submit it to DVS; that route is the program's recommended path but has no matching submission method. No processing time is stated; the instructions (WY-S6) only say to call or email if there has been no letter or call within 30 days after mailing, which is a status-check prompt, not a decision time. Required documents also vary by expense type in the guidelines (gas and lodging receipts for travel, itemized lists for items taken as evidence, physician verification for lost wages past 30 days); only the general ones and the wage and counseling forms are encoded. Privacy: W.S. 1-40-107(d) (from the DVS-posted copy of the Act, WY-S4) makes claim file information that is subject to a confidentiality privilege confidential and not open to public inspection; the protection is tied to information already privileged under Wyoming law, so it is not a blanket rule covering every field on the application. Wyoming has no address confidentiality program, so no substitute-address rule is encoded. The closest thing found is W.S. 35-21-112, a court confidentiality order for a domestic violence victim's address in protection order proceedings, which is not a substitute-address program and was not saved or encoded. Separately, W.S. 6-2-309(m) (WY-S8) keeps sexual assault exam results confidential healthcare information unless the victim signs a release, which is about exam records, not compensation records.

rules.summary: Police, a hospital, or anyone else may not make a sexual assault survivor age 16 or older pay for the evidence exam, directly or through their health insurance.
rules.quote: A law enforcement agency, health care facility, or other entity may not require a victim of sexual assault under AS 11.41.410 — 11.41.425 who is 16 years of age or older to pay, directly or indirectly, through health insurance or any other means, for the costs of examination of the victim necessary for (1) collecting evidence using the sexual assault examination kit under AS 18.68.010 or otherwise; or (2) determining whether a sexual assault has occurred.
rules.source_title: AS 18.68.010 to 18.68.040, Sexual Assault Examinations (Alaska Statutes, print view)

rules.summary: The Alaska Department of Law's victims' rights handbook says sexual assault exams are provided at no cost to victims, and cites AS 18.68.040.
rules.quote: Victims of sexual assaults should obtain sexual assault examinations as soon as possible after the crime has occurred. These exams are provided at no cost to victims [AS 18.68.040].

rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

rules.summary: The application must be made within two years after the date of the injury.
rules.quote: the application has been made within two years after the date of the personal injury or death
rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

params.extension: Applicants past two years are asked to explain the delay; the statute itself sets two years.

rules.summary: The program asks for an application within two years of the crime, and asks applicants who are past two years to explain the delay.
rules.quote: Even if you do not know all related expenses, it is important to open an application within two years of when the crime occurred. If the crime occurred more than two years ago, please provide an explanation as to why there was a delay in requesting financial assistance.
rules.pinpoint: VCCB home page, When to request compensation?
rules.source_title: Alaska Violent Crimes Compensation Board, home page

params.exception: or, if you could not reasonably report that soon, within 5 days of when you could

rules.summary: The crime must be reported to police within five days. If it could not reasonably be reported that soon, it must be reported within five days of when it reasonably could be.
rules.quote: the personal injury or death was the result of an incident or offense listed in AS 18.67.101 that had been reported to the police within five days of its occurrence or, if the incident or offense could not reasonably have been reported within that period, within five days of the time when a report could reasonably have been made
rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

rules.summary: The board can pay only if it finds that the applicant cooperated with police and prosecutors when that was appropriate.
rules.quote: in the discretion of the board, the applicant has cooperated with law enforcement and prosecution officials to further prosecution of the offender if appropriate
rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

params.scope: prosecution or conviction, not the police report

rules.summary: An award can be made even if no one is prosecuted or convicted.
rules.quote: An order may be made under this section whether or not a person is prosecuted or convicted of an offense arising out of the act that caused the injury or death involved in the application.
rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

rules.summary: The board pays only for losses not already covered by the offender, a government, or a private source such as insurance.
rules.quote: the board may award compensation for losses and expenses allowable under AS 18.67.110 for which the applicant is not compensated by the offender or a person on behalf of the offender, or by the United States, a state, or any of its subdivisions or agencies, or a private source
rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

rules.summary: The program pays after insurance and other sources.
rules.quote: VCCB is a payor of last resort.
rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Billing and Payments (providers)

rules.summary: The board considers whether the victim's own behavior contributed to the injury.
rules.quote: In determining whether to make an order under this section, the board shall consider all circumstances determined to be relevant, including provocation, consent, or any other behavior of the victim that directly or indirectly contributed to the victim's injury or death
rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

rules.summary: In sexual assault claims, the board may not deny an award based on the victim's behavior, alcohol or drug use, or social history (the exact protection depends on whether the offender is convicted).
rules.quote: if a claim is based on a crime involving domestic violence or on a crime of sexual abuse of a minor or sexual assault and the offender is (A) convicted of one of those crimes, notwithstanding (1) — (3) of this subsection, the board may not deny an order based on considerations of provocation, the use of alcohol or drugs by the victim, or the prior social history of the victim; or (B) not convicted of one of those crimes, the board may not deny an order based on the involvement or behavior of the victim.
rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

rules.summary: No award may be made if the victim broke a state criminal law in a way that caused or contributed to the injury.
rules.quote: violated a penal law of the state, which violation caused or contributed to the victim's injuries or death
rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

rules.summary: If compensation is probable and waiting would cause undue hardship, the board can make an emergency award of up to $5,000, which is deducted from the final award.
rules.quote: the amount of the emergency compensation may not exceed $5,000
rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

rules.summary: A direct victim's initial counseling award covers up to 24 sessions. The first evaluation and intake session is paid in full, and later sessions with a licensed mental health provider are paid up to $200 each. More sessions can be requested with a treatment plan.
rules.quote: Counseling – Direct Victims: Initial maximum award is 24 sessions. Secondary Victims: initial maximum 12 sessions VCCB will pay first evaluation and intake session in full. Payment after first session: $200/session for services provided by a licensed mental health provider
rules.pinpoint: VCCB Benefits at a Glance, Mental Health Therapy, Payment Maximums
rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Benefits at a Glance (last revised July 2026)

rules.summary: Lost wages are paid at 85% of gross pay, up to $10,000.
rules.quote: Up to $10,000 Compensation is reimbursed at a rate of 85% of gross pay.
rules.pinpoint: VCCB Benefits at a Glance, Loss of Earnings
rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Benefits at a Glance (last revised July 2026)

params.item: work time already covered by paid leave

rules.summary: Lost wage payments cover only leave without pay, not days already covered by paid leave.
rules.quote: Compensation is limited to leave without pay.

rules.summary: Relocation is capped at $7,500 per household ($4,000 for limited income).
rules.quote: Household limit is $7,500 (reduced to $4,000 for limited income), subject to verification of actual expenses.

rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Request for Crime-Related Relocation Assistance (04/2026)

rules.summary: As part of relocation, a motel or hotel stay is paid for up to 5 days at up to $225 per night, including tax and fees.

rules.summary: Chiropractic care is covered for up to 20 visits within 12 months of the crime, up to $3,500. This is a limit on chiropractic only, not on medical care in general.
rules.quote: Chiropractic care: 20 visits within 12 months of crime. Up to $3,500.
rules.pinpoint: VCCB Benefits at a Glance, Medical
rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Benefits at a Glance (last revised July 2026)

rules.summary: A security system and monitoring are paid up to $1,500.
rules.quote: Security system and monitoring: Up to $1,500.
rules.pinpoint: VCCB Benefits at a Glance, Security Measures
rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Benefits at a Glance (last revised July 2026)

rules.summary: Securing doors, windows, and locks is paid up to $4,000.
rules.quote: Securing doors, windows, and locks: Up to $4,000.
rules.pinpoint: VCCB Benefits at a Glance, Security Measures
rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Benefits at a Glance (last revised July 2026)

rules.summary: A destroyed or damaged cell phone is paid up to $1,000.
rules.quote: Destroyed/damaged cell phone: Up to $1,000.

rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Benefits at a Glance (last revised July 2026)

rules.quote: Cell phone (damaged or taken for evidence)

rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB Application for Crime Victim Compensation (05/2026)

rules.summary: Bedding, clothing, and other essential items taken by police as evidence are replaced up to $1,500; a phone is handled separately up to $1,000.
rules.quote: Up to $1,500 Cell phone: Up to $1,000 (not included in $1500 max – see security).
rules.pinpoint: VCCB Benefits at a Glance, Items Taken as Evidence
rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Benefits at a Glance (last revised July 2026)

rules.summary: Crime scene clean-up in a private residence is paid up to $7,000.
rules.quote: Up to $7,000 The police report will be key to verify damage to homes requiring clean-up.
rules.pinpoint: VCCB Benefits at a Glance, Crime Scene Clean-up
rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Benefits at a Glance (last revised July 2026)

rules.summary: Short-term rent help to stabilize housing after the crime is paid up to $4,000 or 2 months, whichever is less, directly to the landlord.

rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Benefits at a Glance (last revised July 2026)

rules.quote: Dental/medical

rules.quote: Counseling/therapy

rules.quote: Travel/transportation

rules.quote: Crime scene cleanup

params.item: property loss or damage (general)

rules.summary: Property loss or damage is generally not covered; essential items taken as evidence (and phones) are limited exceptions.

params.note: Reports from treating or examining physicians, if reasonably available

rules.source_title: AS 18.67.010 to 18.67.180, Violent Crimes Compensation Board (Alaska Statutes, print view)

params.note: Only when claiming lost wages; the VCCB contacts the employer for wage and date information

rules.quote: Your employer will be contacted for wage and date information, however no details of your case will be shared

params.note: Treatment plan, only for counseling beyond the initial award

rules.quote: there are session rate limits and treatment plans are required for services beyond the initial award

rules.source_title: Alaska VCCB, Application and Forms page

params.note: Request for Relocation Assistance form, only when asking for relocation, completed before any relocation expense is covered

params.note: Request for Rental Assistance form plus documentation such as a copy of the lease, only when asking for rental assistance
